title: When a pod's emptyDir exceeds the resource limit, the pod will restart and enter the ContainerStatusUnknown state.
body:
### What happened?

When a pod's emptyDir exceeds the resource limit, the pod will restart and enter the ContainerStatusUnknown state.

### What did you expect to happen?

After the emptyDir of the pod exceeds the resource limit, the pod should enter the error state, should not restart and enter the ContainerStatusUnknown state 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

step1
```
$ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: centos
  labels:
    app: centos
spec:
  containers:
    - name: centos
      image: centos:7
      imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
      command:
        - "/bin/bash"
        - "-c"
        - "sleep 1000000"
      volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /data
          name: tm
      resources:
        limits:
          ephemeral-storage: 100M
  volumes:
    - name: tm
      emptyDir: {}
  restartPolicy: Always
EOF
```
step2

```
$ kubectl exec centos /usr/bin/dd if=/dev/zero of=/data/test bs=1M count=150
```

```

title: topologySpreadConstraints with DoNotSchedule and bad AZ leads to 7/9 pending in that AZ
body:

- create deployment with 9 replicase and AZ spread with DoNotSchedule and maxSkew 1

```

```

### What did you expect to happen?

3/9 being pending in the bad AZ

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

      kind: Deployment
      metadata:
        name: donotschedule
        namespace: kube-public
        labels:
          role: donotschedule
      spec:
        replicas: 9
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            role: donotschedule
        template:
          metadata:
            labels:
              role: donotschedule
          spec:
            topologySpreadConstraints:
            - labelSelector:
                matchLabels:

              topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone

              resources:
                requests:
                  cpu: 0.1

No, 1 az has no nodes without enough free cpu capacity while the others have some.
The nodes in all azs have enough memory/cpu to fit the pod if they were empty/

```
Node:                 <none>
Status:               Pending
...
Topology Spread Constraints:  topology.kubernetes.io/zone:DoNotSchedule when max skew 1 is exceeded for selector pod-template-hash=69fb6f5469,role=donotschedule
...
  Warning  FailedScheduling  46s   default-scheduler  0/17 nodes are available: 1 Insufficient cpu, 1 node(s) had untolerated taint {node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable: }, 10 node(s) had untolerated taint {ownedby: compute}, 11 node(s) didn't match pod topology spread constraints, 3 node(s) had untolerated taint {node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane: true}, 6 node(s) were unschedulable. preemption: not eligible due to preemptionPolicy=Never.
```

Ah, ok, I misunderstood the situation. Thanks for sharing the detail.
Then, the answer is that everything is working expectedly from the scheduler's PoV.

The scheduler basically schedules pending Pods one by one. It doesn't take any other pending Pods into consideration during scheduling.

So, in your scenario, 
1. the scheduler scheduled the first two Pods to different zone's Nodes.
2. the scheduler wanted to schedule the next one to the third zone, but Pods couldn't go due to insufficient resources.
3. All other Pods got unschedulable in the same reason.
4. As a result, 2 went to Nodes, and other couldn't go anywhere.

Yeah, that sounds about right.
So a possible fix would be to make the scheduler look at pending pods too.

Current behavior is bad when 1 az is in trouble and then suddenly the whole app is down, only semi-fix I found so far was to cordon the whole AZ and then use "nodeTaintsPolicy: Honor", but that means manual effort and another restart for all pods.

I wouldn't say the current behavior is wrong.
Because if it goes as your expectation (`3/9 being pending in the bad AZ`), it obviously violates the `maxSkew`.

> Current behavior is bad when 1 az is in trouble and then suddenly the whole app is down

But, this is true. If one az has trouble, that affects the scheduling on other zones as well.
So, probably, what we want to have is something like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105977.

I think the behaviour may be correct in the sense that it is what is documented but I think it would be much more useful to consider Pending pods in the calculation. This is because I think the expectation when someone is setting maxSkew to 1 with replicas 9 is that if one of three AZ is down is that they would still have 6 pods running not that they would be limited to only 2 pods.

I was talking about the current documented behavior, Yes. And, as the past me mentioned, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105977 is necessary if we want the scheduler to behave like your thought. (which I've been hoping to implement for a long time, but pending due to SIG-Autoscaling's bandwidth for reviewing KEP.)

> if one of three AZ is down is that they would still have 6 pods running not that they would be limited to only 2 pods.

Actually, "one of three AZ is down" is a bit different from what I was assuming for this issue, which defined the situation like "1 of the AZs have insufficient capacity".

In your case, if all nodes within one AZ facing issue have taints properly, you can just use `nodeTaintsPolicy: Honor` and then your scheduler should ignore all nodes in the dead AZ at the spreading calculation, and schedule all your pods into two healthy AZs evenly.

I think my point was more that I think it still makes sense to schedule pods to an AZ even "maxSkew" might be exceeded provided that after all the Pending pods are scheduled the skew is less than maxSkew. It seems relatively easy to compute just check `<pods in AZ + 1> < <max Skew>  + <total pods> / <domains>`. I agree that would be a change but I don't understand how anyone could depend on the previous behaviour.

In our case I think it makes sense to use three StatefulSets because that also solves some edge cases around scaling as because of a PVC we can't "move" pods between AZs.

First, as you mentioned, we cannot break this existing behavior in the first place. We'd need an API so that people can opt-in the behavior only if they want, and otherwise keep the current behavior. 

Second, from a technical perspective, the scheduler doesn't know which pods belong to the same group. It just schedules pods one by one and don't consider other pending pods.

Let's say pod-a has this constraint:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod-a
  labels:
    app: awesome-app
spec:
...
          topologySpreadConstraints:
            - labelSelector:
                matchLabels:
                  app: awesome-app
              maxSkew: 1
              topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
              whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
```

Then, if we want to compute like your formula, how would it get `<total pods>`? It's not correct to assume pods with `app: awesome-app` label as `<total pods>` because maybe not all pods with the label have the constraint. 

And, third, from the behavior perspective, why do we still want to keep 2 pods pending (in your scenario)? I know the current behavior is worse because it only allows only 2 pods to be scheduled, while keeping 7 pods pending. 
But, I believe the ideal behavior, in general, is to just spread pods evenly on _available_ AZs for reliability. For example, people just want to keep pods spread across all available AZs so that the service can be reliable even when one AZ is dead. And then, when one AZ is actually dead, they probably wouldn't want to keep pods in one AZ pending, but they would expect them to be scheduled on other AZs instead of a dead AZ so that the service gets a full replicas coming back soon even after one AZ's issue.
That's why I'm saying let's wait for https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105977 (or use `nodeTaintsPolicy`, although that involves the troublesomeness of putting taints onto all nodes in the dead AZ). It's simpler and more aligned with that expectation; people define their pods can be fallback to other AZs in such cases. In your scenario, if one AZ is dead, all pods would go to two alive AZs evenly, not keeping two pods pending.

Also, sidenote though, Pod Topology Spread is already one of the slowest in-tree plugins. So, for that reason as well, we don't want to put additional calculations basically in it.

That makes sense I think the part I wasn't aware of was that the plugin is only aware of the scheduled pods.

I think there's cases with Volumes that are tied to an AZ where you wouldn't want to fallback to different zones and without the Descheduler it would mean that it still recover after. I do concede though it doesn't look really practical to change this though and there are other ways to solve the issue.

I may be confusing RFC-1123 and RFC-1035 label name requirements:
```
RFC 1123 Label Names
Some resource types require their names to follow the DNS label standard as defined in [RFC 1123](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc1123). This means the name must:

contain at most 63 characters
contain only lowercase alphanumeric characters or '-'
start with an alphanumeric character
end with an alphanumeric character
RFC 1035 Label Names
Some resource types require their names to follow the DNS label standard as defined in [RFC 1035](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc1035). This means the name must:

contain at most 63 characters
contain only lowercase alphanumeric characters or '-'
start with an alphabetic character
end with an alphanumeric character
```

It seems that only RFC-1035 requires that the first character be alphabetic. My underlying issue is that a Java client is reporting that a customer's URL contains an "unsupported URI."

Hello @niranjandarshann ,

I think the reason for your pods being in Pending state is because the `local storage` path does not exist on the required node as per the affinity, i.e. `kubenode01`. Please ensure that a directory named `/store` is created on `kubenode01`, before creating the persistent volume i.e before running `kubectl apply -f PVdemo.yml`. Also, fields like volumeName and volumeMode are not required in the pvcdemo.yaml file.

I used the following commands to create a directory and provide it necessary permissions on node matching affinity rules:
`mkdir -p /mnt/disk/store`
`chmod 777 /mnt/disk/store`

Please also make sure the storage-class parameters are as listed below, before creating persistent volume:
``` javascript
kind: StorageClass
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: local-storage
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
```
In case of local storage, usually your persistent volume claim should remain in pending state, due to `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer`, as that is required for local storage. Your PV-claim should not be listed as `Bound` as soon as it is created. It should be listed as `Pending`, as shown below:

``` javascript
NAME             STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS    AGE
pvc-demo-final   Pending                                      local-storage   5s
```

Here's the final set of yml files I have used from your sample and the pod is running fine as expected.
`Note`: There are very minor differences in yml as you may notice like node name is different(my cluster env), removed unnecessary fields from pvcdemo.yaml , changed port from 8080 to 80 for nginx and used nginx:alpine image instead of `niranjandarshan/bihartour:latest` in pod.

Here's the set of YAML files:
PVdemo.yaml
```javascript
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pv-demo-final
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  volumeMode: Filesystem
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: local-storage
  local:
    path: /store
  nodeAffinity:
    required:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
      - matchExpressions:
        - key: kubernetes.io/hostname
          operator: In
          values:
          - staging-worker


```


pvcdemo.yaml
```javascript

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pvc-demo-final
spec:
  storageClassName: local-storage
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Mi

```

Poddemo.yaml
```javascript

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: pod-with-pvc-demo-final
  labels:
    name: pod-with-pvc-demo-final
spec:
  containers:
  - name: pod-with-pvc-demo
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
      name: podport
    volumeMounts:
    -  name: persistent-storage
       mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
  volumes:
  -  name: persistent-storage
     persistentVolumeClaim:
       claimName: pvc-demo-final


```

I also created an index.html at /store location in my worker node(matching the node affinity), since I was using nginx. This allowed me to curl pod IP after pod is in running stage, to ensure the storage is mounted successfully and is being served as an HTML page for nginx.

Hopefully. these updates to your yaml file will provide the necessary fix for you. 

I have the pod running at my end :
```javascript
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE                NODE             NOMINATED NODE  
pod-with-pvc-demo-final   1/1     Running   0          91s      staging-worker              <none>

```
So,to summarise, it seems like in your case, it's a mix of a couple of things :
a. Was `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` used in storage class for local storage ?
b. Has `/store` directory with necessary permissions been created on kubenode01 before creating persistent volume ? 
c. Remove volume mode and volume name from persistent volume claim. This should not be required.

Hopefully , this can resolve the issue at your end and we should be able to close this issue soon .

Thanks

So, there's not many things I can think of, which may have caused your issues , but we can try these:

2. Also, can you please list your nodes and pods and please run the following command :

title: Deployment rolling update stucked with pod anti-affinity
body:
### What happened?

Use case: only have 3 nodes available in cluster, a deployment with pod anti-affinity yaml like this:
```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  replicas: 3
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - labelSelector:
                matchExpressions:
                  - key: app
                    operator: In
                    values:
                      - nginx
              topologyKey: "kubernetes.io/hostname"
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.7.9
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

After applied, the pods running ok.
But if the image changed to `nginx:1.8.1`, then apply again, the newly created pod will be pending, with event like this:
```
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  25m   default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) didn't match pod affinity/anti-affinity, 3 node(s) didn't satisfy existing pods anti-affinity rules.
  Warning  FailedScheduling  23m   default-scheduler  0/3 nodes are available: 3 node(s) didn't match pod affinity/anti-affinity, 3 node(s) didn't satisfy existing pods anti-affinity rules.
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Expect to roll update deployment pods to desired state without stuck (pending).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See description above.

### Anything else we need to know?

Tested other workloads statefulset and daemonset, they both work ok in this senario.

Hello @astraw99 ,

I will try to explain what's happening here and will also share a fix with you for this problem.

The pod `Anti-affinity` rule used in the deployment , is a typical way to spread your pods on unique cluster nodes.  Since, there were no pods with selector `app=nginx`, when you created the deployment for the very first time, it ran successfully and Kubernetes was able to place the pod on separate cluster nodes. 

However, when you update the image of the deployment to 1.8.1, a new deployment rollout kicks in. Since, the default rollout strategy is `RollingUpdate`, and default `max surge is 25%` , the Replicaset can be scaled up to a point so that total number of old and new pods do not exceed 125% of desired pods. An absolute number in this case will probably be one(1) extra pod for rolling update going through each pod one by one.
Now, the problem arises , when you have 3 pods running already , all on separate nodes, a new pod is created by the ReplicaSet Controller(because of max surge property) and it cannot be scheduled by the scheduler to any available nodes, because of your pre-defined `anti-affinity` rule. Since, the rule simply states that each node can only have 1 pod matching selector `app=nginx` , your deployment gets stuck forever. 

To fix this issue, the following needs to be added in your deployment yaml under `strategy`:
```javascript
 replicas: 3
 ..
 ..
 strategy:
   rollingUpdate:
     maxSurge: 0
     maxUnavailable: 1
   type: RollingUpdate

```


The key lies in the `maxSurge` field here. Once, we have set `maxSurge` as zero , we are basically conveying to Kubernetes that you must not add a new pod to do a rollout. Rather, please take down an existing pod and this gets satisfied by also adding the `maxUnavailable` property as 1.
This ensures, that for each rollout of pod, atmost only one pod gets deleted and is unavailable. Once a pod is removed, the new pod can be easily rolled out again on a node, because now the `anti-affinity rule` works again, as there is no pod with matching selector `app=nginx`  case on atleast one node each time.

Please refer to the following steps which confirm that this works: (Deployment with the maxSurge=0 and maxUnavailable=1)
```javascript

kubectl apply -f deployment.yml && kubectl get pods -o wide (stripping out IPs etc.)

NAME                                READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE      NODE
nginx-deployment-67c9f8555f-9b67w   1/1     Running   0          2m42s    staging-worker-2
nginx-deployment-67c9f8555f-fj8pq   1/1     Running   0          2m42s    staging-control-plane
nginx-deployment-67c9f8555f-mgr6l   1/1     Running   0          2m42s    staging-worker-1

kubectl set image deploy nginx-deployment nginx=nginx:1.8.1 && kubectl rollout status deploy nginx-deployment
deployment.apps/nginx-deployment image updated
Waiting for deployment "nginx-deployment" rollout to finish: 0 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "nginx-deployment" rollout to finish: 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "nginx-deployment" rollout to finish: 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "nginx-deployment" rollout to finish: 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "nginx-deployment" rollout to finish: 2 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "nginx-deployment" rollout to finish: 2 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "nginx-deployment" rollout to finish: 2 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
Waiting for deployment "nginx-deployment" rollout to finish: 2 of 3 updated replicas are available...
deployment "nginx-deployment" successfully rolled out

```

I hope this clarifies why the deployment update was failing and how the fix using `maxSurge` can help in preserving the anti-affinity rule in this case. Hope this is helpful.

nodes.title: Fix deployment deadlock with antiPodAffinity
nodes.body:
When surge is active (allPodsCount > desired replicas) and maxUnavailable rounds to 0, old pods cannot scale down, blocking new pods with antiPodAffinity constraints.

Enforce minimum maxUnavailable of 1 in this scenario to prevent deadlock.

Fixes #116891


#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug


#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR fixes a deadlock scenario in deployment rolling updates when using pod anti-affinity rules.

The default surge and `maxUnavailable` is 25%, so basically if we use anti-affinity we get the deadlock described in #116891. When maxUnavailable rounds to 0 (e.g., with 3 replicas and 25% unavailable) while surge is active, the deployment controller won’t scale down old pods because `maxUnavailable=0`, but new pods can’t schedule because anti-affinity rules conflict with the existing old pods. This creates a permanent deadlock where the rollout never completes.

The fix enforces a minimum of 1 for `maxUnavailable` when we detect that surge is active (more pods exist than desired) and `maxUnavailable` has rounded to 0. This allows at least one old pod to be removed, making room for new pods to schedule.
#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes #116891

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
I’ve added logic in the deployment sync controller to detect when we’re in a surge state with maxUnavailable=0. The fix is minimal and only affects this specific case. normal deployment behavior remains unchanged.
I've also added some unit tests to test it works correctly.
#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
NONE
```release-note
Fixed deployment rolling update deadlock when maxUnavailable rounds to 0 and pod anti-affinity prevents new pods from scheduling alongside old pods.
```

title: PodAntiAffinity prevents scheduling the only pod with the label in AntiAffinity
body:
### What happened?

I created a deployment that looked as follows:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  labels:
    app: test
  name: test
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  strategy: {}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - podAffinityTerm:
              labelSelector:
                matchExpressions:
                - key: app
                  operator: In
                  values:
                  - test
              topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
            weight: 100
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - labelSelector:
              matchExpressions:
              - key: app
                operator: In
                values:
                - test
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      containers:
      - image: nginx
        name: nginx
```

It successfully created a pod in my one node kind cluster:

```
$ k get pod
NAME                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
test-84dc5648f7-hbprp   1/1     Running   0          22s
```

I then realized that I want `podAntiAffinity` just within an image version, so I added a new label for that, making the deployment look like this:

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  labels:
    app: test
  name: test
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: test
  strategy: {}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: test
        app-version: v0
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - podAffinityTerm:
              labelSelector:
                matchExpressions:
                - key: app-version
                  operator: In
                  values:
                  - v0
              topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
            weight: 100
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - labelSelector:
              matchExpressions:
              - key: app-version
                operator: In
                values:
                - v0
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      containers:
      - image: nginx
        name: nginx
```

I applied it and found that the new pod can not be scheduled:

```
$ k get pod
NAME                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
test-6cf566dbb7-8jfxq   0/1     Pending   0          3s
test-84dc5648f7-hbprp   1/1     Running   0          117s
```

Looking at the event, it seems to be because of the affinity:

```
$ k describe pod test-6cf566dbb7-8jfxq|rg Warn
  Warning  FailedScheduling  46s   default-scheduler  0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't satisfy existing pods anti-affinity rules. preemption: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod.
```

This doesn't make sense to me, as the only pod in the cluster that has the label used by the `podAntiAffinity` is the one that is now in pending:

```
$ k get pod -l app-version -A
NAMESPACE   NAME                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
default     test-6cf566dbb7-8jfxq   0/1     Pending   0          89s
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The new pod that uses the new label for `podAntiAffinity` to be scheduled onto the existing node, as the existing pod doesn't have the relevant label.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See the `What happened` section

Hmm, so you're setting the ``--resolv-conf`` kubelet flag to ``C:\etc\kubernetes\cni\hostdns.conf`` flag, consuming that file. Right now, we're expecting that flag to be either an empty string ``""`` or ``Host``, and kubeadm also sets that flag to ``""`` [1].

This PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/110566 introduced the capability to read the DNS config options from the Windows host registries while removing the capability to read from a file, introducing a regression. I've sent a PR addressing this issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116800

[1] https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c9ff2866682432075da1a961bc5c3f681b34c8ea/cmd/kubeadm/app/componentconfigs/kubelet_windows.go#L73
@ibabou Is the file you are pointing to a UNIX-style resolv.conf or something else?
Was the file `C:\etc\kubernetes\cni\hostdns.conf` changing the behavior of the node?

Yeah, what used on GCE/GKE, seems to be a Linux-like conf, eg:

`
> cat C:\etc\kubernetes\cni\hostdns.conf
nameserver 10.128.0.1
search c.<project_name>.internal google.internal
`

We haven't tried to remove from kubelet to see the behavior.

title: Trying to create an object that already exists can fail with non "AlreadyExists" errors (e.g. validation)
body:

### What did you expect to happen?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Supose we have a yaml as follows:

# service.yaml
apiVersion: v1

```

/assign @thockin @khenidak 
/sig network

Let's see the different operations and its results 
- `kubectl create -f  service.yaml -v9` you do a POST -- returns 422
- `kubectl apply -f  service.yaml -v9` you do a PATCH -- returns 200 OK
- `kubectl replace -f  service.yaml -v9` you do a PUT -- returns 200 OK

```
[6.5.8](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7231#section-6.5.8).  409 Conflict

   The 409 (Conflict) status code indicates that the request could not
   be completed due to a conflict with the current state of the target
   resource.  This code is used in situations where the user might be
   able to resolve the conflict and resubmit the request.  The server
   SHOULD generate a payload that includes enough information for a user
   to recognize the source of the conflict.

   Conflicts are most likely to occur in response to a PUT request.  For
   example, if versioning were being used and the representation being
   PUT included changes to a resource that conflict with those made by
   an earlier (third-party) request, the origin server might use a 409
   response to indicate that it can't complete the request.  In this
   case, the response representation would likely contain information
   useful for merging the differences based on the revision history.
```

you are trying to recreate the resources, not to update it, update works ok.
I feel that this status code is correct, but my knowledge in this area is limited

/cc @liggitt @thockin @khenidak
@aojea   But if I change `nodePort: 30123` to another port, it will return 409 as expected.  obviously，it verify whether it is legal before verifying whether it exists.
What really matters is that reason is `FieldValueInvalid` not `AlreadyExists`, Is this intentional?

> What really matters is that reason is `FieldValueInvalid` not `AlreadyExists`, Is this intentional?

I can't really say, but this NodePort and ClusterIP allocation went through a big refactor recently and I would not think is intentional 

I think that this error is raised here 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fe91bc257b505eb6057eb50b9c550a7c63e9fb91/pkg/registry/core/service/storage/alloc.go#L531

it seems that we should indeed check that is a conflict error and return `AlreadyExists` as you point out

```$ k get -o yaml pod iamyouare-5849d6b47-gg9sl | kubectl create -f -
Error from server (AlreadyExists): error when creating "STDIN": pods "iamyouare-5849d6b47-gg9sl" already exists, the server was not able to generate a unique name for the object

$ k get -o yaml service iamyouare | kubectl create -f -
The Service "iamyouare" is invalid: spec.clusterIPs: Invalid value: []string{"10.0.176.164"}: failed to allocate IP 10.0.176.164: provided IP is already allocated
```

That is fun.  Even if I force a validation error in the pod, I get "AlreadyExists".  I don't know exactly why, except that Service uses some uncommon paths through the apiserver.  Digging a bit...

staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/registry/generic/registry/store.go `func (e *Store) Create()` calls `e.BeginCreate()` which is what is failing in this allocation.  We don't know until much later if the name already exists, but I don't know where, exactly.

Later in Create() we call `BeforeCreate()` which calls validation.  If validation fails, we can get the same sort of error on pods:

```
$ k get -o yaml pod iamyouare-5849d6b47-gg9sl \
    | sed 's/restartPolicy:.*/restartPolicy: foobar/' \
    | sed 's/generateName:.*//' \
    | kubectl --validate=false create -f -
The Pod "iamyouare-5849d6b47-gg9sl" is invalid: spec.restartPolicy: Unsupported value: "foobar": supported values: "Always", "OnFailure", "Never"
```

So this is not unique to Service.

@deads2k @lavalamp 
/sig api-machinery

Some  clients like [fabric8io/kubernetes-client](https://github.com/fabric8io/kubernetes-client)  will offer function like createOrReplace which will call create (post)first ,then judge whether the HTTP code  equal 409 (HTTP_CONFLICT), if so call replace(put). Like codes below

https://github.com/fabric8io/kubernetes-client/blob/43531077d3d67d3b4fd300e2e4e0b0e4b231229c/kubernetes-client/src/main/java/io/fabric8/kubernetes/client/utils/internal/CreateOrReplaceHelper.java#L42-L66

It  will go wrong In the above scenario,because the apiserver return `422`.

Actually creating an object has to be a last step, and that's the only point at which we find out if the name is reserved. If something turns up wrong before we get to that step, we can't even attempt to store the object to find that it already exists.

You might think that we could just check if the object exists to begin with, but the case above is still possible in a race.

For better behavior, use SSA -- it probably will do what you were hoping for.

> For better behavior, use SSA -- it probably will do what you were hoping for.

Yes，server-side-apply can satisfy my needs.

/triage accepted
/close
Please feel free to reopen it if needed.

title: If it is "Not-Applicable" for external IP point to have a value, then `kubectl get services` should display 'N/A' instead of '<none>'
body:
### What happened?

I am trying to learn k8s and following along in the official tutorials
https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/kubernetes-basics/expose/expose-interactive/

Why is the endpoint empty? The tutorial says that

> We have now a running Service called kubernetes-bootcamp. Here we see
> that the Service received a unique cluster-IP, an internal port and an
> **external-IP (the IP of the Node)**


I only see `<none>` . 

_"External-IP is `<none>` when there is no load balancer" (Sander Van Vugt)_

If it is "Not-Applicable" for external IP point to have a value, then `kubectl get services` should display 'N/A' instead of '`<none>`'. Having `<none>` tells me that something went wrong or was incomplete. 

```
    $ kubectl expose deployment/kubernetes-bootcamp --type="NodePort" --port 8080
    service/kubernetes-bootcamp exposed
    
    $ kubectl get services
    NAME                  TYPE        CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)          AGE
    kubernetes            ClusterIP   10.96.0.1      <none>        443/TCP          9m13s
    kubernetes-bootcamp   NodePort    10.101.46.87   <none>        8080:30568/TCP   7m49s
    
    $ kubectl describe services/kubernetes-bootcamp
    Name:                     kubernetes-bootcamp
    Namespace:                default
    Labels:                   app=kubernetes-bootcamp
    Annotations:              <none>
    Selector:                 app=kubernetes-bootcamp

    IP Families:              <none>

    IPs:                      10.101.46.87

    NodePort:                 <unset>  30568/TCP

    kubernetes-bootcamp   NodePort    10.101.46.87   **<none>**        8080:30568/TCP   7m49s

### What did you expect to happen?

You _can_ set `externalIP` for a clusterIP service, e.g. 
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: netdebug4
spec:
  selector:
    vmService: vmcalicobridge2
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 22
  externalIPs:
    - 1.2.3.4
```
So "N/A" would be wrong IMO. It _is_ applicable, you just haven't set any extenal IPs (there can be many).
/assign @shaneutt

Hi @1dropaflame thanks for sending in an issue :wave: 

We discussed this one on our SIG Network community meeting today and along with @aojea and @uablrek's comments above, the general opinion seems to lean towards `<none>` being a fine way to indicate that the `Service` has no external IPs. In fact to expand on @uablrek's comment: `Services` can actually have their type _changed_ to `LoadBalancer` from `ClusterIP` after creation meaning an external IP can be assigned later. It's not fully clear why a change is needed here, is this causing some kind of problem? Can you help us to better understand the impetus for change?
Thank you for the information that an external IP can be assigned later on, and that the consensus is to leave it as-is. I shall close the issue. :)

title: Mutation of a cached object in kubelet through in place resizing of pods
body:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/76d351065e504e23b7962158ef0e9067b6bd96ed/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2682

mutates the pod object in place (vs creating a copy first).  That's illegal and can cause data races or potentially panics (the panic is unlikely here but I can't rule it out).

This line should be:

```
pod = updatedPod
...
kl.podManager.UpdatePod(pod)
```

This should be fixed because we might serialize the object in the middle of this from somewhere else and if the object changes midway the protobuf object we create may not be valid, leading to panics in kubelets with this gate turned on.

/sig node
/priority critical-urgent
/kind bug
/assign @vinaykul 

### What did you expect to happen?

No mutation of pod objects from within `Sync*Pod` methods (in fact no mutation of `pod` should occur in most loops).

title: ServiceAccount not getting deleted as a child resource when another object has the same uid
body:
### What happened?

When I create ServiceAccount as a child resource of other resources, and delete the parent resource, the ServiceAccount did not get deleted.

To illustrate I made a small demo based on [this official blog](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2021/05/14/using-finalizers-to-control-deletion/#owner-references):

A parent ConfigMap:

```console
$ cat <<EOF | kubectl create -f -
> apiVersion: v1
> kind: ConfigMap
> metadata:
>   name: mymap-parent
> EOF
configmap/mymap-parent created
```
Get the uid of the parent ConfigMap:

```console
$ CM_UID=$(kubectl get configmap mymap-parent -o jsonpath="{.metadata.uid}")
```

A child ConfigMap:

```console
$ cat <<EOF | kubectl create -f -
> apiVersion: v1
> kind: ConfigMap
> metadata:
>   name: mymap-child
>   ownerReferences:
>   - apiVersion: v1
>     kind: ConfigMap
>     name: mymap-parent
>     uid: $CM_UID
> EOF
configmap/mymap-child created
```

A child ServiceAccount:

```console
$ cat <<EOF | kubectl create -f -
> apiVersion: v1
> kind: ServiceAccount
> metadata:
>   name: mysa-child
>   ownerReferences:
>   - apiVersion: v1
>     kind: ConfigMap
>     name: mymap-parent
>     uid: $CM_UID
> EOF
serviceaccount/mysa-child created
```

List the ConfigMaps:

```console
$ kubectl get cm
NAME                                DATA   AGE
mymap-child                         0      3m16s
mymap-parent                        0      3m25s
```

List the ServiceAccounts:

```console
$ kubectl get sa
NAME         SECRETS   AGE
default      0         25d
mysa-child   0         4m41s
```

Delete the parent ConfigMap:

```console
$ kubectl delete cm mymap-parent
configmap "mymap-parent" deleted
```

The child ConfigMap got correctly deleted:

```console
$ kubectl get cm
NAME                                DATA   AGE
```

But the child ServiceAccount was not:

```console
$ kubectl get sa
NAME         SECRETS   AGE
default      0         25d
mysa-child   0         4m41s
```


### What did you expect to happen?

The ServiceAccount get deleted with the parent resource.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

  uid: 965967ae-a944-4e69-95c8-46fdb4d8327a

$ kubectl get profile/ksa.default.mysa-child -o yaml
apiVersion: projectcalico.org/v3
kind: Profile
metadata:
  creationTimestamp: "2023-03-17T06:43:37Z"
  name: ksa.default.mysa-child
  resourceVersion: /18769347
  uid: 965967ae-a944-4e69-95c8-46fdb4d8327a
spec:
  labelsToApply:
    pcsa.projectcalico.org/name: mysa-child
```

But it seems that the garbage collector tries to gc the `profile/ksa.default.mysa-child` as a child resource of the parent ConfigMap?

I saw the comment about the calico API server reusing the same UID for two different objects at https://github.com/projectcalico/calico/issues/5715#issuecomment-1473676706

That is incorrect and will definitely break the garbage collector, sometimes flakily depending on which object was observed first. 

Closing this since that seems like the cause of this flake.

title: MatchConditions webhooks can be bypassed by injecting a very expensive match condition before others
body:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116261#discussion_r1132819194

If any match condition fails the request should not be sent to the webhook but if a very large condition uses up all the evaluation time before the webhook fail condition is reached the request will fallback to the fail policy and matchCondition will not bypass the result

### What did you expect to happen?

Fail match condition bypasses webhook call

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Write a very expensive match condition that evaluates for infinity and then a match condition that should return false after it in the match condition order.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: API-initiated eviction does not work on first try in certain scenarios, but does work on second try
body:
### What happened?

Scenarios that require setting resourceVersion either

- explicitly to the eviction request
- or when the eviction API needs to make sure that the pod has not become ready when deleting unready pods https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/registry/core/pod/storage/eviction.go#L232

fails to evict a pod. This is caused by a conflict with PodDisruptionConditions feature, which adds a condition to a pod, and the delete itself fails. The second eviction works correctly and results in a pod deletion.

### What did you expect to happen?

eviction should succeed on a first try 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a simple pod

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  containers:
    - name:  nginx
      image: registry.k8s.io/nginx-slim:0.8
```

```
$ kubectl apply -f nginx.yaml
```

2. obtain its resource version

```
$ kubectl get pod nginx -oyaml | grep resourceVersion
> resourceVersion: "313"
```

3. try to evict it

```
$ kubectl create -f - <<EOF --raw /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/nginx/eviction
{"apiVersion": "policy/v1", "kind": "Eviction", "metadata": {"name": "nginx"}, "deleteOptions": {"preconditions": {"resourceVersion": "313"}}}
EOF
$ Error from server (Conflict): Operation cannot be fulfilled on Pod "nginx": the ResourceVersion in the precondition (313) does not match the ResourceVersion in record (425). The object might have been modified
```

the eviction request fails, but we can see that the DisruptionTarget condition has been added to the pod

```
$ oc get pod nginx -oyaml | grep DisruptionTarget -B 5
>   - lastProbeTime: null
>    lastTransitionTime: "2023-03-13T21:29:04Z"
>    message: 'Eviction API: evicting'
>    reason: EvictionByEvictionAPI
>    status: "False"
>    type: DisruptionTarget
```

4. second eviction with updated resouce version succeeds


```
$ kubectl create -f - <<EOF --raw /api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/nginx/eviction
{"apiVersion": "policy/v1", "kind": "Eviction", "metadata": {"name": "nginx"}, "deleteOptions": {"preconditions": {"resourceVersion": "520"}}}
EOF
> {"kind":"Status","apiVersion":"v1","metadata":{},"status":"Success","code":201}
```

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

This is obviously not ipvs bug. The column OutPkts (3rd column) of the ipvsadm printout is always 0 in your test. It means that SYN-ACK was not routed through ipvs on the way back to pod1, and thus ipvs did not have chance to perform SNAT for the packet. That's why it has pod2 (instead of clusterIP) as srcIP.

This is a clear indication of route setting issue, not ipvs bug. You can compare the ipvs stats between working and non-working case for confirmation. 

As you mentioned the same traffic case ran ok from the begging, I guess, the route configuration in `kube-proxy` perhaps was manipulated due to some changes in your k8s cluster during runtime, leading to this problem.

For further troubleshooting, you can check kube-proxy.log to see if any new events that could trigger the problem. You can also capture the printouts below and compare the same printout between working and non-working case to see if any route entries or iptables rules are missing:
```
iptables -t nat -S

title: Transition running deleted pods to a terminal phase
body:
### What happened?

Running pods when deleted are not transitioned to a terminal phase, even when all containers are terminated. Note that, containers are not restarted for deleted pods: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L73-L77.

This is problematic for jobs, which as a workaround categorizes all deleted pods (with `deletionTimestamp != nil`) as failed,
but it is still problematic:
- the replacement pod is created too early, leaving two running pods (for the same index) at the same time, which is a problem for some job frameworks. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.
- a pod categorized a failed by the job controller (due to the presence of deletionTimestamp) may end up succeeded if the pod's container completes successfully within the graceful termination period. 
- it blocks a related issue in Jobs: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855.

The solution might be scoped to pods with finalizers to save a PATCH request to make the transitioning. 

Fixing this issue is planned as part of the Jobs KEP: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329

### What did you expect to happen?

Every deleted running pod is transitioned to a terminal phase if there is a finalizer.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a pod like this:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: running-pod
  finalizers: ["example.com/my-finalizer"]
spec:
  restartPolicy: Always
  containers:
  - name: main
    image: centos:7
    command: ["bash"]
    args: ["-c", 'echo "Hello world" && sleep 1800']
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
```
2. Delete the pod by `kubectl delete`
After 30s check the pod status with `kubectl get pods -oyaml`. You can see:

```yaml
    containerStatuses:
    - ...
      state:
        terminated:
          exitCode: 137
          reason: Error
    phase: Running
```
**Issue**: the pod remains the in the **Running** phase forever.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This is needed to make sure all pods are eventually transitioned to a terminal phase (Failed or Succeeded). Currently, running pods with RestartPolicy equals `OnFailure` or `Always` are not transitioned to a terminal phase. 
The case for `OnFailure` is problematic for jobs:
-  currently workaround to determine if a pod is failed by looking at the `deletionTimestamp` to determine if a pod is failed (which can actually end up succeeded). See related Issue:  
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/113855 (superseded by https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/116858). 
- the replacement pod is created too early in some scenarios. See related Issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115844.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
<!--
*Automatically closes linked issue when PR is merged.
Usage: `Fixes #<issue number>`, or `Fixes (paste link of issue)`.

-->
- Tracking issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/3329
- Fixes: #116410

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

This PR extends the scope from the PR to transition not only Pending pods, but also Running.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
<!--

For more information on release notes see: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/release-notes.md
-->
```release-note
Give terminal phase correctly to all pods that will not be restarted. 

In particular, assign Failed phase to pods which are deleted while pending. Also, assign a terminal 
phase (Succeeded or Failed, depending on the exit statuses of the pod containers) to pods which
are deleted while running.

This fixes the issue for jobs using pod failure policy (with JobPodFailurePolicy and PodDisruptionConditions 
feature gates enabled) that their pods could get stuck in the pending phase when deleted.

ACTION REQUIRED: Users who maintain controllers which relied on the fact that pods with RestartPolicy=Always
never enter the Succeeded phase may need to adapt their controllers. This is because as a consequence of 
the change pods which use RestartPolicy=Always may end up in the Succeeded phase in two scenarios: pod 
deletion and graceful node shutdown.
```

title: InPlacePodVerticalScaling CI tests fail due to parallel tests stepping over each other in low CPU count CI system
body:
### What happened?

In-place pod resize CI tests were re-enabled in PR https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/pull/28928 following merge of PR #102884  These tests are failing and the root cause appears to be pods timing out awaiting scheduling, Unschedulable due to  Insufficient cpu.

Running these tests in serial is a quick way to address the problem. It can be followed by a better fix.

### What did you expect to happen?

All in-place pod resize E2E tests should pass in CI.

title: service account creation with restricted RBAC not working
body:
### What happened?

Hi, 
I have a following role and rolebinding definition. I want to allow the service account creation only with specific resource names. 

Example: I should able to create  service account using `dev-blue` with the name `dev-green` and vice versa.
If I am trying to create a service account with any other names it should fail but at the moment  i am unable create service account using `dev-blue` with the name `dev-green` and vice versa.

```
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: main-role
  namespace: dev
rules:
- apiGroups:
  - ""
  resources:
  - serviceaccounts
  verbs:
  - create
  - delete
  - get
  - list
  - patch
  - update
  resourceNames:
  - dev-blue
  - dev-green
  ---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: dev-rolebinding
  namespace: dev
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: dev-green
    namespace: dev
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: dev-blue
    namespace: dev
  ---
  ---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: dev-blue
  namespace: dev
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: dev-blue
  namespace: dev
  annotations:
    kubernetes.io/service-account.name: dev-blue
type: kubernetes.io/service-account-token
  ```

### What did you expect to happen?

 I should able to create  service account using `dev-blue` with the name `dev-green` and vice versa.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. apply the role and role binding
2. try to create a service account with the name dev-green using service account dev-blue.

### Anything else we need to know?

title: Static pod resources are double counted in kubelet admission because mirror pods are not excluded
body:
### What happened?

When a new pod is admitted to the Kubelet, it is compared to all other "active" pods.  Active pods are the set of pods that have been observed from a config set, minus those that have already failed admission or are in a terminal phase (as the Kubelet sees it).  This check is performed by `Kubelet.GetActivePods()` and calls `kl.filterOutInactivePods()` on the contents of podManager.

During review of #113145 I was reminded that pod manager contains three sets of pods:

* Pods created via the API that are desired to run on this node (API pods)
* Pods created via local config sources that are desired to run on this node (static pods)
* Pods created on the API by the Kubelet to represent static pods (mirror pods)

For every static pod there should be one mirror pod in the API, but sometimes they lag (if the API is down or slow).  Mirror pods are not source of truth - if a Kubelet sees a mirror pod coming from the API it will take no action on it.  So today when we calculate the resources in use on a Kubelet in admission we are double counting the contribution from a single static pod if the mirror pod already exists (such as when a Kubelet is restarted).

This doesn't impact *new* static pods, but it does impact updated static pods which are typically modelled as delete -> recreate (for various reasons) and pods that are created after static pods.  This is similar to #104824 in that the Kubelet needs to be very careful when performing admission to correctly account for *all* resources in use, not just the list of desired pods.  Finally, because we perform pod name exclusion on pods (we don't run two pods with different UIDs but the same pod fullname at the same time), we should also consider the impact of admitting a pod that maps to another pod by full name - it will not be running at the same time.  This is most relevant for force deleted pods - a new one can be created and rescheduled to the same node and cannot start until the old pod is done.

In general, the Kubelet is bad at reconciling admission decisions after the fact (eviction is not 100% feature equivalent to admission) and so we need to either get better at that reconciliation or be more aggressive on pod rejection (the latter is more disruptive to users, but also better for health).  We should also consider whether static pods should be admitted automatically for some decisions.

/sig node

### What did you expect to happen?

We need to correctly account for resources running on the node.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create a static pod that uses 50% of a resource on the node.  Wait until the mirror pod is created.  Attempt to schedule a pod to the node that uses 1% of that resource.   

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

All recent.

_No response_

title: Service publishNotReadyAddresses and EndpointSlices Conditions
body:
The EndpointSlice API says

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fafa45d13c21dcf99801631413fc58e9cf91226c/pkg/apis/discovery/types.go#L111-L116

and it works as expected in normal circumstances

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: terminating
  labels:
    app: MyApp
spec:
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 300
  containers:
  - name: agnhost
    image: k8s.gcr.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.39
    args:
      - netexec
      - --http-port=80
      - --delay-shutdown=300
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: terminating-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: MyApp
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
```

I delete the pod and the endpoints conditions are the expected
```
    ready: false
    serving: true
    terminating: true
```

However, if during this time I set `service.spec.publishNotReadyAddresses: true` 

```
    ready: true
    serving: true
    terminating: true
```

we run into an incoherence with the API doc, but it seems that we already documented this edge case in the code

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fafa45d13c21dcf99801631413fc58e9cf91226c/pkg/controller/endpointslice/utils.go#L44-L60

I think that at this point is just to amend this information to the API, no? 

```diff
diff --git a/pkg/apis/discovery/types.go b/pkg/apis/discovery/types.go
index efc2d331ec9..1a19ad5ecaa 100644
--- a/pkg/apis/discovery/types.go
+++ b/pkg/apis/discovery/types.go
@@ -112,7 +112,8 @@ type EndpointConditions struct {
        // according to whatever system is managing the endpoint. A nil value
        // indicates an unknown state. In most cases consumers should interpret this
        // unknown state as ready. For compatibility reasons, ready should never be
-       // "true" for terminating endpoints.
+       // "true" for terminating endpoints, except when the Service associated has
+       // enabled the field PublishNotReadyAddresses.
        Ready *bool
 
```

/kind bug
/kind documentation

title: VPA panics in standalone kubelets
body:
1. Start a standalone kubelet (not registered to an API server)

2. Manager construction short-circuits `Start()` here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/253ab3eda71f250ad6692bb16f035cebaf0651c9/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L186-L192

3. VPA state is never initialized here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/253ab3eda71f250ad6692bb16f035cebaf0651c9/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L195-L200

4. All pod syncs then panic on this line:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a1b12e49eac237a37939642d0c3395008b9ab380/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2412

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x18 pc=0x3b5f21f]
k8s.io/kubernetes/pkg/kubelet.(*Kubelet).HandlePodAdditions(0xc00073c400, {0xc001816c00?, 0x27, 0x40})
  pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go:2412 +0x4df
```

_Originally posted by @liggitt in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/102884#issuecomment-1454089210_

cc @thockin @vinaykul
/sig node
/kind bug
/priority important-soon

the panic I saw wasn't on Windows, it was on Linux, but while spelunking, I saw another possible panic. On Windows, NewPodContainerManager() returns:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ead7d66ee12656cfb7c633dd42a87f8d9cfaa469/pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_windows.go#L183-L185

> I want to understand why this is even getting to doPodResizeAction.

that certainly is surprising and suggests that something in computePodResizeAction may not be correct in standalone cases or for static pods

> I will do a defensive fix (skipcomputePodResizeAction and doPodResizeAction for static pods)

I don't really know if making exceptions for static pods is correct when running against an API server where we're reporting status of used resources. @smarterclayton, would you expect an updated manifest that changes resources to be handled by VPA?

> > I want to understand why this is even getting to doPodResizeAction.
> 
> that certainly is surprising and suggests that something in computePodResizeAction may not be correct in standalone cases or for static pods

Yes, that's what I want to get to the bottom of.

I suspect that for some reason, computePodResizeAction incorrectly determined that a resize is necessary for a best effort pod or burstable w/o CPU limits pod (which resulted in NP access due to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ead7d66ee12656cfb7c633dd42a87f8d9cfaa469/pkg/kubelet/cm/helpers_linux.go#L167L189 )

`computePodResizeAction` is a pretty complex function that needs to correctly account for various states a container may be in (not running, restarting etc) and I need a repro to ensure any fix I make actually works as intended.

> > I will do a defensive fix (skipcomputePodResizeAction and doPodResizeAction for static pods)
> 
> I don't really know if making exceptions for static pods is correct when running against an API server where we're reporting status of used resources. @smarterclayton, would you expect an updated manifest that changes resources to be handled by VPA?

When I tried this last time by updating the manifest resources and saving it (just out of curiosity) , I found that pod was restarted (not patched - which triggers the resize workflow). But I don't know if it should be officially supported.

I don't have a repro (attempted testing it without skipping computePodResizeAction / doPodResizeAction for static pods) in local cluster + kubeletonly with either best effort static pod or burstable static pod with cpu requests specified. 

Do you have the pod yaml that caused this issue in your env?
not offhand, I'd have to spin up a cluster manually and try to binary search the static manifests we use to isolate it, and I have negative time to dig with code freeze reviews :-/

> . @smarterclayton, would you expect an updated manifest that changes resources to be handled by VPA?

If you mean, when VPA points at a mirror pod can it change spec?  No, generally.  If you mean, should static pod consumed resources be visible via the API?  Yes.

> If you mean, when VPA points at a mirror pod can it change spec? No, generally.

From what we can tell, *something* in the VPA path (`computePodResizeAction `) thought a static pod's resources needed to trigger the resize code path.

I don't know enough about static pod handling to know if that is a category error and VPA should *never* expect to resize resources used by static pods. That's what part of the proposed fix in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116504 does - excludes static pods from being considered by VPA.

For a kubelet running against an API server, would you expect manifest-driven pods to be able to make use of resize functionality? If so, a blanket exclusion of static pods from that code path doesn't seem correct.

> > . @smarterclayton, would you expect an updated manifest that changes resources to be handled by VPA?
> 
> If you mean, when VPA points at a mirror pod can it change spec? No, generally. If you mean, should static pod consumed resources be visible via the API? Yes.

I think the implementation can support resizing static pods via patch to its mirror. There is some bug in the pod update -> pod worker sync handoff where the resize update is lost. IMHO, we should allow resizing static pods as well via its mirror. (Standalone kubelet is a different story - the current implementation terminates and adds new pod). We just haven't considered this scenario and it needs a bit of work (mainly to develop solid e2e test cases for mirror pod resize and standalone scenario). This is something I'd want to take the time to fix the right way in 1.28, so my preference is to make a defensive fix for v1.27 (aka we don't support static pod resizing for 1.27 alpha) rather than trying to wing it.

In HandlePodUpdates, static pods are processed by handleMirrorPod:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fcf5d23e6818ccfbc92f332af82f31661f8d4f88/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2491-L2502
which dispatches SyncPodUpdate for the original pod, and not the updated mirror pod.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fcf5d23e6818ccfbc92f332af82f31661f8d4f88/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L2412-L2420

For normal pods, SyncPodUpdate is invoked for the updated pods. This is the reason (bug) I didn't see resize updates come through in SyncPod().

I don't know how long the code has been this way, but I'm hesitant and risk-averse to just swap out `pod` with `mirrorPod` so close to code freeze. This is why I feel it is best to disable static pods for resize at this time and do it right in 1.28

> I'm hesitant and risk-averse to just swap out `pod` with `mirrorPod` so close to code freeze.

Agreed on not making big changes right before code-freeze. Can you open a tracking issue for that and tag @smarterclayton @bobbypage on it?

> This is why I feel it is best to disable static pods for resize at this time and do it right in 1.28

As commented in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116504#discussion_r1134868462, it seems like the static pod carve-outs and feature gate checks are leaving gaps in that series of `if` statements relative to 1.26 handling event when the feature is disabled... at the very least, it's really hard to reason about, which is not what we want from feature-gated isolated code

I think that PR needs to be made more obviously isolated / no-op when the feature gate is disabled, or we should consider dropping VPA out of 1.27
Tracking issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/116597 where the repro steps try updating container image of a static pod (no involvement of in-place resize feature)

About excluding computePodResizeAction and doPodResizeAction for static pods, I did try 'update manifest and save' and found that pod was being removed and added with updated spec (with FG enabled). I'll verify again with traditional (non debugger) methods for FG enabled & disabled cases ... we are thin on pre-submit signals for this change.

> > If you mean, when VPA points at a mirror pod can it change spec? No, generally.
> 
> From what we can tell, _something_ in the VPA path (`computePodResizeAction `) thought a static pod's resources needed to trigger the resize code path.
> 
> I don't know enough about static pod handling to know if that is a category error and VPA should _never_ expect to resize resources used by static pods. That's what part of the proposed fix in #116504 does - excludes static pods from being considered by VPA.
> 
> For a kubelet running against an API server, would you expect manifest-driven pods to be able to make use of resize functionality? If so, a blanket exclusion of static pods from that code path doesn't seem correct.

From sig-node discussion just now, it sounds like updating mirror to effect changes to the pod is discouraged. We probably should be more explicit and block in validation if there are no sound reasons to allow updates to static pods via api. With that discussion, and given current state with https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/116597 , my change to exclude static pods for computePodResizeAction and doPodResizeAction is not only defensive but may also be the right fix.

I'll verify standalone kubelet manually for FG enabled/disabled cases later after my meeting with Clayton.

/cc @derekwaynecarr @dchen1107 @SergeyKanzhelev

title: kubectl apply requires CRDs to apply non-CRD resources if we use `kind: List`
body:
### What happened?

kubectl apply performs validation before the apply. 

Non-CRD resources (e.g. pods / deployments) don't need CRD schema for validation, but if we use `kind: List` resource, kubectl calls `LIST apis/apiextensions.k8s.io/v1/customresourcedefinitions`.

nodes.title: Skip hasSupport check for List type
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Currently, when user applies a List type resource, there is an unnecessary request to customresourcedefinitions endpoint by validation. The reason of this request is that validation can not find List type in OpenAPI schema and behaves this type as CRD.

This PR returns unsupported when List type is applied.

In terms of functionality, there is no bug or any issue, because eventually `schemaValidation` detects this List and executes `validateList` function. Only issue is unnecessary CRD enpoint request.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #116245

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
None
```

```

### What did you expect to happen?

The scheduler should not crash.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I don't have a small reproduction because it only happens when the scheduler is under sudden stress. However, I have a simulated data set locally (dumped from production, so I can't share) that I can load into a fake apiserver ([kube-scheduler-simulator](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kube-scheduler-simulator)) and I confirmed that this same crash happens every time for that data set.

> Deployed multinode cluster, in primary cp node, can see kubelet client certificate (/var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-client-current.pem) has a validity of 10yrs but in other node has a validity of 1yr.

changing the kubeadm cert expiration constant is not recommended. 

during bootstrap. for kubeadm init, kubeadm must sign the kubelet cert manually. for join, it uses the kubelet setting of 1 year. this process is by design.

IIRC, the kubelet setting one year is not customizable.

you can just leave the kubelet to auto rotate certs each year (default) or sign them manually, like "kubeadm init phase kubeconfig kubelet" and then "kubeadm init phase kubelet-finalize"

/kind support

title: unstable map iteration order causes test to sometimes leave non-GA features disabled
body:
### What happened?

PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/115324 was reverted by #116062 because it (erroneously) relied on OpenAPIV3 feature to be enabled, but `TestPodSecurityGAOnly` would non-deterministically leave the feature disabled after running.

I tracked it down to the fact that this test disables all `PreRelease` or `Beta` features in a loop which iterates over a `map`, which are known to have unstable iteration order:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e55f2a9b54e0f6bd9ed12e50752d7d2545ab0cab/test/integration/auth/podsecurity_test.go#L74-L81

When key `AllBeta` is processed before key `OpenAPIV3`, then `AllBeta` would disable `OpenAPIV3` before `OpenAPIV3`s default value is to be saved.

Normally, `AllBeta` ignores features that have been explicitly set, so it only affects those which fall back on the `Default` value. But this issue does not just affect `OpenAPIV3` but any non-GA feature.

I suggest the loop in `TestPodSecurityGAOnly` be made to skip the special feature keys such as `AllBeta`.

/cc @liggitt 
/cc @apel

### What did you expect to happen?

The value before every feature gate should be restored after running `TestPodSecurityGAOnly`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This test always fails on my machine (just pasted it into `test/integration/auth/podsecurity_test.go`):

```go
func TestRestoreFeatures(t *testing.T) {
	var targetFeature featuregate.Feature

	// Grab a beta feature form the list to test with
	for k, v := range utilfeature.DefaultMutableFeatureGate.GetAll() {
		if v.PreRelease == featuregate.Beta && v.Default {
			targetFeature = k
			break
		}
	}

	if len(targetFeature) == 0 {
		t.Log("no beta features to test against")
		return
	}

        // see if we iterate the feature map with AllBeta first within a few tries
	for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
		attemptFunc := func() bool {
			fg := utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.DeepCopy()
			originalValue := fg.Enabled(targetFeature)

			func() {
				// Disable all alpha and beta features
				for k, v := range fg.DeepCopy().GetAll() {
					if v.PreRelease == featuregate.Alpha || v.PreRelease == featuregate.Beta {
						defer featuregatetesting.SetFeatureGateDuringTest(t, fg, k, false)()
					}
				}
			}()

			return originalValue != fg.Enabled(targetFeature)
		}

		if attemptFunc() {
			t.Fatal("original value for feature not same as new value after restoration")
			break
		}
	}
}
```

A pod using gpu in our k8s cluster, when we delete kubelet_internal_checkpoint and restart the node where the pod is located. After the node start normally, we find that, the pod is running, but the gpu device is not mounted on the container of pod. If we delete container of the pod, the gpu device mount normally.
I think the reason is that the pod is start befor gpu device register right to kubelet.

 In the function  allocateContainerResources,  if isDevicePluginResource return false, kubelet will skip device allocation, however, if the device plugin not register right to kubelet and the kubelet_internal_checkpoint is lost, the function isDevicePluginResource will reture false, and generate the problem report.

title: Cacher may not send events if it reinitializes at the time of watch initialization
body:
Found when reviewing https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116024

I'm still not 100% convinced it's true, but I believe this is a faulty scenario:
1. new watch is being established `Watch()` method
2. `c.ready` is still initialized so we successfully pass the c.ready.wait() check
3. `ListAndWatch` in `startCaching` fails (for whatever reason)
4. `c.ready.set(false)` is called (from defer in `startCaching`)
5. `startCaching` is called again and we call `terminateAllWatchers()`
6. the Watch call (started in point 1 above) only now continues to be processed and is established (and added to watchers) - init events are being send in the meantime
7. `ListAndWatch` is being called from `startCaching` which reinitializes watchCache to a new (higher RV)
8. if some events missed in the meantime, they will not be delivered to this newly established watch

/kind bug
/priority critical-urgent
/sig api-machinery

nodes.body: /triage accepted

title: PVs with annotations are not being dynamically provisioned on k8s 1.26.1
body:
### What happened?

We observed that when deplying manifests to a cluster running 1.26.1-gke.200, the StorageClass and PVC get created successfully. However, the PVC is stuck in a Pending state and no PV is provisioned.

The workaround is to add storageClassName to one of the pending PVCs on cluster, and it did go from Pending to properly provisioned a PV and reaching Bound state. 

We looked at the logs and found that according to the doc: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes/#class,

```
In the past, the annotation volume.beta.kubernetes.io/storage-class 
was used instead of the storageClassName attribute. This annotation
 is still working; however, it will become fully deprecated in a future 
Kubernetes release.
```

Is this annotation is fully deprecated in the new 1.26.1 release? If yes can we add this detail to documentation or release note?






### What did you expect to happen?

the PVC should not stuck in a Pending state and PV is provisioned in 1.26.1

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a 1.26.1-gke.200 cluster in GKE
2. Create via yaml

```
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: sunnytest-sc
parameters:
  type: pd-ssd
provisioner: kubernetes.io/gce-pd
reclaimPolicy: Delete
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: storage-class-issue-test
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: storage-class-issue-test
  serviceName: storage-class-issue-test
  replicas: 1
  template:

title: kube-proxy IPVS mode: traffic sent from pods to an external LoadBalancer IP is NOT directed to the respective cluster IP instead
body:
### What happened?


According to the [docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-proxy/#:~:text=will%20be%20masqueraded%20and-,traffic%20sent%20from%20pods%20to%20an%20external%20LoadBalancer%20IP%20will%20be%20directed%20to%20the%20respective%20cluster%20IP%20instead.,-For%20dual)  

> traffic sent from pods to an external LoadBalancer IP will be directed to the respective cluster IP instead

But in fact it's not the case for kube-proxy running in IPVS mode.

### What did you expect to happen?


This is kind of "breaking change" that IPVS mode brings - **pods running on the nodes, where there are no pods which Loadbalancer IP's related service points to, are capable to access that service by External IP (e.g. Ingresses that are resolved in DNS to LoadBalancer IP)**:
1. only if `ExternalTrafficPolicy` for related service is set to `Cluster`
2. only via SrcNAT loosing their IPs in logs

There are no such limitaions with kube-proxy in `iptables` mode which provide redirection to ClusterIP mentioned above via iptables rules with comments like _"Redirect pods trying to reach external loadbalancer VIP to clusterIP"_

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Any installation with kube-proxy in IPVS mode

Please, be aware that access to a loadBalancerIP with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` from a _POD in main netns_ (hostNetwork: true) will still fail if there are no local endpoints. From other PODs it works.

> Note that pods and nodes are allowed to connect to services via load balancer IPs. Ideally, pod-to-load-balancer-IP connections should be "short circuited" to the cluster IP by the service proxy, to ensure that the source IP can be preserved. (If the connection was not short-circuited, then normally the connection would end up SNAT'ed to the node IP before being passed to the load balancer.)
> ...
> (There is a subtle interaction here with the "short circuit" behavior of pod-to-load-balancer traffic: the behavior when a pod connects to a load balancer IP should logically be the same whether the service proxy short circuits it or not. Thus, when a pod connects to an `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` service via its load balancer IP, the connection must succeed _even if the pod is on a node with no endpoints for that service_.)

nodes.title: One lock among PodNominator and SchedulingQueue
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The PodNominator stores the same `*QueuedPodInfo` objects as the `*SchedulingQueue`, while having each their own lock.
Given that `QueuedPodInfo` objects can be updated due to Pod changes while a scheduling cycle access the PodNominator, we should share the lock among them. This happens in the preemption path.

title: client-go/cache: informer misses delete events on relist for elements only present in the queue
body:
### What happened?

For quite a while we have seen that some controllers/informers suddenly get out of sync with the state of the world, and keep `x` (different number every time).

After more investigation, we think we narrowed it down to the informer having a queue of events while a relist occur, and for some objects, we never see the `DELETED` event. This leads to a leak of some sort, and the informer is stuck in a bad state. The informers in question have resyncs disabled, so this only goes back to normal after a new relist. It should be noted that the queue at the point of the relist have been `1000`+ elements, so the controller are clearly in a state where they are lagging very far behind.

### What did you expect to happen?

Overall we expect that after a reflector relist, no objects should be stuck in a dangling state where they are added to the informer store, but never cleared; even when they are no longer present in k8s.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

A rough timeline about what we think happens;
```
1. new Object is added O, agent gets CREATED event for it
2. watch is terminated, and the agent runs a new list, L
3. CREATE event for O is still on the queue to be processed.
4. informer replaces the old data in store with L, and O is not in L
  - Since O is not in the store, and not in the list L, no DELETED event is queued
5. CREATE event for O is still on the queue to be processed.
6. CREATE event for O is processed
7. O is <leaked>; its present in the agents external "store" (and I assume also the internal informer store) but not in k8s.
```

I've been trying to write an informer/controller test to reproduce, but its kinda tricky since it depends on the ordering the `DeltaFIFO.Replace` and `DeltaFIFO.Pop` functions are able to acquire the `DeltaFIFO` lock.

### Anything else we need to know?

~Given this is indeed the case, I assume this would affect all users of informers, and most heavily those with the resync period set to `0`, aka. disabled.~. After some digging, I think the opposite is true. Since resyncs won't refetch the list from k8s, it will just put all the cached object on the queue, slowing down processing even more; possibly causing even more leaks.

```console
$ kubectl version
