To spell it out a little more: the bug is that the behavior of `func (f *DeltaFIFO) Replace(list ...)` was leaving an entry in `f.queue` and `f.items` if it was there beforehand and absent from `list` and `f.knownObjects`.  This is consistent with the comments on DeltaFIFO::Replace but is not the behavior that suits the clients (informers); it would cause this ghost item to later (when the DeltaFIFO's Pop method is called) get added to the informer's local cache and delivered in a notification to the informer's client(s).

[1]: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/77c7d6d36cbc3cd16762ff093be575aa3d2ceed0/pkg/k8s/informer/informer.go#L103

adding to 1.27 and marking as a blocker to resolve before release (not because it's necessarily urgent to resolve today, just so it doesn't get lost/forgotten)... it's unclear to me if the change that was already merged is acceptable for 1.27, or if it needs rework to avoid breaking existing delta/informer consumers

Thanks @liggitt! I'm also scratching my head here, because there were already code paths doing the same inside the `DeltaFIFO` before this patch, so its possible to "reproduce" the same behavior on eg. `v1.26.0` as well. Its not clear to me if more people are doing this code of "object cleanup" after popping deltas tho., especially since people haven't noticed the previous leak, or the strange behavior when not having a backing store/`knownObjects`.

Made a quick reproduction test here; https://github.com/odinuge/kubernetes/commit/e15eb7ee0669f7eead07317f6b714f01780db0f6

By uncommenting the line; `//*test = testFifoObject{}`, one can mimic the behavior in cilium.

Tho cilium is using a backing store like other informers, so if one provides `knownObjects` to the `DeltaFIFO` and uncomments out that line, it will;
- on `v1.26.0`; not create a delete event at all.
- on `master`; create a delete event with an object that is "empty"/cleared out.

I'll think some more tomorrow

Hmm. Maybe we have to use the latest object in `knownObjects` to get around this in case people mutate the deltas, and just pop the key from the queue when its not present in `knownObjects`, and we have some elements in the queue; stupid basic proof-of-concept for it here; https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116190. Maybe this has other side effects tho?

I guess the most important thing we should do is figure out if we support users mutating the objects they pop from the queue, and if so, writes some tests verifying that we handle it gracefully.

The tests looked pretty good to me, it should keep the most recent known object and that's what it seems to do.

Judging from the code you linked, I think cilium should stop mutating the object passed in the notification. The code does NOT expect objects in deltas or the store to be modified out of band. Maybe an easy fix is for them to make a copy before processing the notification?
have we swept in-tree code to make sure we don't have any similar issues?

I think the object in the Deltas{} gets directly placed in the store, and we use a mutation cache in tests to detect that that doesn't get modified, so, I'm at least 30% sure that we don't do this in-tree
Also hitting this with Calico controllers on very large clusters. Is anyone aware of a workaround while this is getting merged? Enable resync? Empty queue faster?

The condition for hitting the problem should be very rare but if your environment is triggering it I think it'll be hard to tweak the environment to make it stop. > The current state as I understand it is that the k8s go client library change fixes the bug, but cilium is mutating objects in place and needs to fix that before they'll be able to use the new library. @odinuge is that correct?

### What happened?

After pod is ready, Liveness probe and Readiness probe detection fails, displaying:

  Warning  Unhealthy  21m (x49 over 2d1h)  kubelet  Readiness probe failed: Get "http://10.244.54.71:18051/healthcheck": context deadline exceeded (Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers)
```
This kind of phenomenon happens by accident. Maybe after some time, the event will disappear.
I want to know what is the root cause of this event？



### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet probe httpGet correctly, no probe failed event report.

```
livenessProbe:
      failureThreshold: 3
      httpGet:
        path: /healthcheck
        port: http
        scheme: HTTP
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 5
      successThreshold: 1
      timeoutSeconds: 30
readinessProbe:
      failureThreshold: 3
      httpGet:
        path: /healthcheck
        port: http
        scheme: HTTP
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 5
      successThreshold: 1
      timeoutSeconds: 30
```
The timeoutSeconds configuration time has been extended to 30s

title: The graduation HPA container resource metrics to beta
body:
### What would you like to be added?

ref: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/1610

This is what we actually need to do for the graduation to beta:

- [x] ⚠️ [bug] change HPA controller to ignore `ContainerResource` when it's disabled by the feature gate. 
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116043
- [x] 🚀 [enhancement] make a difference in `SuccessfulRescale ` events between the resource metric and the container resource metric.
  - Currently, we cannot distinguish the scaling up event between `type: Resource` and `type: ContainerResource`. Both of them create the event like `memory resource utilization (percentage of request) above target` and we cannot know which is the direct reason.
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116045
- [x] 🚀 [enhancement] graduate the feature gate to beta. enabled by default.
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116046
- [x] 📔 [test] the tests to confirm the behavior on switching the feature gate
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116043
- [x] 👁️ [metrics] tracked in separated issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/115639
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116010
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/116326


### Why is this needed?

To satisfy the beta graduation criteria.

/assign
/sig autoscaling

title: Sandbox containers not deleted leaving pods in NotReady state

We have K8s cluster deployed with v1.23.3.

We have a testcase to create a namespace with few resources (few via statefulsets) and then cleanup all the resources by deleting the namespace. It is observed that namespace deletion using "kubectl delete ns <namespace>" deletes the namespace and it successfully displays the message that "Namespace <namespace> is deleted". Upon running "kubectl get pods -n <namespace>", we do not find any pods in that namespace. We expect that upon namespace deletion and pod deletion, all the containers should get deleted successfully so that pod deletion can happen successfully.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Deleting a namespace may trigger this behavior.
It can be triggered by deleting pods directly or via deleting statefulsets/deployments. 
The goal is to delete pods ultimately.
It seems to be happening always in this particular environment of ours.

### Anything else we need to know?

One point to note here is that the kind of testing that is being done on this environment.
The namespaces are first created and then quickly deleted afterwards. This cycle is then repeated.
So, the cleanup of K8s resources is being expected very soon after they are created.
None of our other environments have this type of requirement where so frequent creation/deletion is expected.

Found the solution:

The reason for the pods are showing NotReady after they are dead is, the dead containers associated with them are not immediately cleaned up and garbage collected. The garbage collection of the containers are dependent on 3 flags -- https://pwittrock.github.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/kubelet-garbage-collection/ .

**1.	minimum-container-ttl-duration
2.	maximum-dead-containers-per-container
3.	maximum-dead-containers**  

By default the value of maximum-dead-containers is -1, which means any number of dead containers can be existed in the w node after they are dead.
By default the value of maximum-dead-containers-per-container is 1, means for one particular pod maximum 1 dead container can be existed in the w node.

I have made the following change in the /usr/local/lib/systemd/system/**kubelet.service** file in all the worker nodes.

**--maximum-dead-containers=1**
and
**--maximum-dead-containers-per-container=0**

And after that **daemon-reload** and **restarted the kubelet service**.

All NotReady pods are gone!

/close

- [16/Jan/2023:12:57:39 +0000] "DELETE /proxy/apiserver/apis/flowcontrol.apiserver.k8s.io/v1beta2/prioritylevelconfigurations/e2e-testing-prioritylevel HTTP/1.1" 200 176 "-" "e2e.test/v1.23.13 (linux/amd64) kubernetes/592eca0 -- [sig-api-machinery] API priority and fairness should ensure that requests can be classified by adding FlowSchema and PriorityLevelConfiguration" "x.y.z.11" ``` After the checking the code it seems the reason behind is here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/817b9af22eb5a856c5d2bb02f57d5384a7b4cf2c/test/e2e/apimachinery/flowcontrol.go#L282 ``` resp, err := c.CoreV1().RESTClient().Get().RequestURI("/metrics").DoRaw(context.TODO()) ``` https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/817b9af22eb5a856c5d2bb02f57d5384a7b4cf2c/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/rest/request.go#L332 ``` // RequestURI overwrites existing path and parameters with the value of the provided server relative URI. func (r *Request) RequestURI(uri string) *Request { ... ``` the query not use the full path configured in the kube-config, it keeps only the IP:PORT and then add the /metrics. title: Cannot create ingress with ingressClass annotation and IngressClassName both set
body:
### What happened?

An ingress resource with both `kubernetes.io/ingress.class` annotation and `spec.ingressClassName` set cannot be **created**. Ingress resources can be updated to include both the annotation and the `ingressClassName` without issue.

Kubernetes response:

> The Ingress "example-ingress" is invalid: annotations.kubernetes.io/ingress.class: Invalid value: "nginx": can not be set when the class field is also set



### What did you expect to happen?

The ingress should be deployed with both annotation and `spec.ingressClassName` set, as it is supported by updating an existing ingress.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Apply this resource:

```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: example-ingress
  annotations:
    ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
    kubernetes.io/ingress.class: "nginx"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: test.foo.bar
    http:
      paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
          backend:
            service:
              name: dummy-service
              port:
                number: 1234

```

### Anything else we need to know?

The code causing this issue is here:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f166a525737e700d12da56833388af72585d4239/pkg/apis/networking/validation/validation.go#L279

title: Allow PV NodeAffinity to update from beta to GA topology labels
body:
### What happened?

In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114268, we realized that non in-tree PVs can be impacted by a future removal of beta topology labels from Nodes if they are supporting the beta topology labels.

### What did you expect to happen?

title: pod_startup_latency_tracker doesn't track the lastFinishedPulling time
body:
It can be observed in any kubelet log, just pick one from a random job in CI, per example

```sh
$ wget https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-jenkins/pr-logs/pull/114703/pull-kubernetes-e2e-gce/1608841379780235264/artifacts/e2e-022435249c-674b9-minion-group-gdj4/kubelet.log

$ grep tracker kubelet.log  | grep -v " firstStartedPulling=\"0001-01-01" | grep Observed
Dec 30 15:33:06.941831 e2e-022435249c-674b9-minion-group-gdj4 kubelet[8362]: I1230 15:33:06.941726    8362 pod_startup_latency_tracker.go:102] "Observed pod startup duration" pod="kube-system/metadata-proxy-v0.1-d59wc" podStartSLOduration=-9.223372025913092e+09 pod.CreationTimestamp="2022-12-30 15:32:56 +0000 UTC" firstStartedPulling="2022-12-30 15:32:58.409218371 +0000 UTC m=+2.180058389" lastFinishedPulling="0001-01-01 00:00:00 +0000 UTC" observedRunningTime="2022-12-30 15:33:01.628463642 +0000 UTC m=+5.399303661" watchObservedRunningTime="2022-12-30 15:33:06.941684349 +0000 UTC m=+10.712524397"
Dec 30 15:33:13.374424 e2e-022435249c-674b9-minion-group-gdj4 kubelet[8362]: I1230 15:33:13.374400    8362 pod_startup_latency_tracker.go:102] "Observed pod startup duration" pod="kube-system/kube-dns-autoscaler-5f6455f985-n4pqn" podStartSLOduration=-9.223372017480421e+09 pod.CreationTimestamp="2022-12-30 15:32:54 +0000 UTC" firstStartedPulling="2022-12-30 15:33:07.759304457 +0000 UTC m=+11.530144475" lastFinishedPulling="0001-01-01 00:00:00 +0000 UTC" observedRunningTime="2022-12-30 15:33:13.267182708 +0000 UTC m=+17.038022722" watchObservedRunningTime="2022-12-30 15:33:13.374355038 +0000 UTC m=+17.145195062"
Dec 30 15:33:13.375379 e2e-022435249c-674b9-minion-group-gdj4 kubelet[8362]: I1230 15:33:13.375359    8362 pod_startup_latency_tracker.go:102] "Observed pod startup duration" pod="kube-system/konnectivity-agent-gnc9k" podStartSLOduration=-9.223372029479458e+09 pod.CreationTimestamp="2022-12-30 15:33:06 +0000 UTC" firstStartedPulling="2022-12-30 15:33:09.258791695 +0000 UTC m=+13.029631711" lastFinishedPulling="0001-01-01 00:00:00 +0000 UTC" observedRunningTime="2022-12-30 15:33:13.375009262 +0000 UTC m=+17.145849275" watchObservedRunningTime="2022-12-30 15:33:13.375317944 +0000 UTC m=+17.146157970"
```

The `lastFinishedPulling` time is always `0001-01-01 00:00:00 +0000`, that is the golang zero time IIRC.
In addition, when the image is already present, neither `firstStartedPulling` and `lastFinishedPulling` are set.

I think that the fix has to be something like this

```diff
diff --git a/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go b/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go
index 3fbec1f2b56..863e8ccfa98 100644
--- a/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go
+++ b/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go
@@ -134,6 +134,8 @@ func (m *imageManager) EnsureImageExists(ctx context.Context, pod *v1.Pod, conta
        if !shouldPullImage(container, present) {
                if present {
                        msg := fmt.Sprintf("Container image %q already present on machine", container.Image)
+                       m.podPullingTimeRecorder.RecordImageStartedPulling(pod.UID)
+                       m.podPullingTimeRecorder.RecordImageFinishedPulling(pod.UID)
                        m.logIt(ref, v1.EventTypeNormal, events.PulledImage, logPrefix, msg, klog.Info)
                        return imageRef, "", nil
                }
@@ -164,6 +166,7 @@ func (m *imageManager) EnsureImageExists(ctx context.Context, pod *v1.Pod, conta
 
                return "", imagePullResult.err.Error(), ErrImagePull
        }
+       m.podPullingTimeRecorder.RecordImageFinishedPulling(pod.UID)
```

but this means that we are lacking testing on these, feature, I'd expected to see at least 2 new tests in

`pkg/kubelet/util/pod_startup_latency_tracker_test.go`
`pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager_test.go`

/sig node
/kind bug
/help

/cc @bobbypage @azylinski

title: Pod terminating stuck because of trying to umount not actual mounted dir
body:
### What happened?

A status of Pod mounted NFS PV remain as terminating when a node shutdown and restart.

### What did you expect to happen?

A Pod is completely terminated.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

### Summary

- Deploy a Pod mounted NFS PV
- Shutdown the node where the Pod is running
- Wait for 5 min and the Pod status become `Terminating`
- Restart the node
- The Pod status is still `Terminating` and the Pod is never terminated completely

<details>

### Reproduce

Prepare a NFS Server.(I used `nfs-kernel-server`)  

Deploy a Pod mounted NFS PV like this.  
`nfs-pv-test-pod.yaml`
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: nfs-pv-test-pod
  name: nfs-pv-test-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - image: ubuntu
    name: nfs-pv-test-pod
    command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while :; do sleep 10; done"]
    volumeMounts:
      - name: nfs-test-volume
        mountPath: "/srv"
  volumes:
    - name: nfs-test-volume
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: nfs-test-pvc
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/hostname: node02

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: nfs-test-pvc
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Mi

---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: nfs-test-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Mi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteMany
  nfs:
    server: <NFS Server IP Address>
    path: <NFS Server Dir Path>
```

Shutdown the node where the Pod is running.(In this case `node02`)
```console
root@node02:~# shutdown now
```

And the status of node02 becomes `NotReady`.
```console
$ k get no
NAME     STATUS     ROLES           AGE    VERSION
cp01     Ready      control-plane   126d   v1.25.0
node01   Ready      <none>          126d   v1.25.0
node02   NotReady   <none>          126d   v1.25.0
```

After 5 min later(by default), the Pod status becomes `Terminating`.  
(The time a Pod becomes `Terminating` status depends on `tolerationSeconds`.)  
https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/taint-and-toleration/#taint-based-evictions  
```console
$ k get po -owide -w 
NAME                    READY   STATUS        RESTARTS      AGE   IP            NODE     NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES
nfs-pv-test-pod         1/1     Running       0             27m   10.0.160.99   node02   <none>           <none>

nfs-pv-test-pod         1/1     Running       0             28m   10.0.160.99   node02   <none>           <none>
nfs-pv-test-pod         1/1     Terminating   0             33m   10.0.160.99   node02   <none>           <none>
nfs-pv-test-pod         0/1     Terminating   0             38m   <none>        node02   <none>           <none>
nfs-pv-test-pod         0/1     Terminating   0             39m   <none>        node02   <none>           <none>
```

Then, restart the node and the status of node02 becomes `Ready`.
```console
$ k get no
NAME     STATUS     ROLES           AGE    VERSION
cp01     Ready      control-plane   126d   v1.25.0
node01   Ready      <none>          126d   v1.25.0
node02   Ready      <none>          126d   v1.25.0
```

But the Pod status is still `Terminating` and the Pod is never terminated completely.
```console
$ k get po 
NAME                    READY   STATUS        RESTARTS      AGE   IP            NODE     NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES
nfs-pv-test-pod         0/1     Terminating   0             45m   <none>        node02   <none>           <none>
```

It seems that a `kubelet` faild to delete Pod because of trying to unmount a not mounted directory.
```console
$ k describe po nfs-pv-test-pod
Name:                      nfs-pv-test-pod
Namespace:                 default
...
Containers:
  nfs-pv-test-pod:
    Container ID:  containerd://c908fc752e70f5181b3983ce812e51be463cf3bd798d0a9b28cc45b3bb3d9353
    Image:         ubuntu
...
Events:
  Type     Reason         Age   From               Message
  ----     ------         ----  ----               -------
  Normal   Scheduled      10m   default-scheduler  Successfully assigned default/nfs-pv-test-pod to k8s-cluster3-worker02
  Normal   Pulling        10m   kubelet            Pulling image "ubuntu"
  Normal   Pulled         10m   kubelet            Successfully pulled image "ubuntu" in 6.353410672s
  Normal   Created        10m   kubelet            Created container nfs-pv-test-pod
  Normal   Started        10m   kubelet            Started container nfs-pv-test-pod
  Warning  NodeNotReady   9m5s  node-controller    Node is not ready
  Warning  FailedKillPod  56s   kubelet            error killing pod: failed to "KillPodSandbox" for "d695b232-ff16-454a-830b-02194bec6d01" with KillPodSandboxError: "rpc error: code = Unknown desc = failed to destroy network for sandbox \"a078587c537484be9b622a2d1694cfaa3a6a2c6ac83872ca08c0c4758bb82af2\": plugin type=\"calico\" failed (delete): error getting ClusterInformation: Get \"https://10.96.0.1:443/apis/crd.projectcalico.org/v1/clusterinformations/default\": dial tcp 10.96.0.1:443: i/o timeout"

title: kube-scheduler: Bring back the ability to stop at the first failed filter
body:
#108829 changed the default behavior of scheduler framework's `RunFilterPlugins` - from stopping at the first failed filter to always running all filters. This change breaks Cluster Autoscaler at scale. Cluster Autoscaler imports the scheduler framework to simulate filters on artificial nodes. In a (pretty common) one-pod-per-node scenario, the number of `RunFilterPlugins` calls is ~quadratic wrt. the number of nodes needed for unschedulable pods - it can be a lot of calls. Before #108829, in such scenario the vast majority of `RunFilterPlugins` calls would stop at failing Fit or NodeAffinity filters, and not run the rest of them (e.g. PV-related filters). After the change, every call to `RunFilterPlugins` runs all filters, which completely breaks Cluster Autoscaler at scale (an example scenario of 300 1-pod-per-node pods and 200 node groups takes >10min in 1.24, and ~50s in <1.22).

Can we get the old behavior back? Or re-introduce the config option so that Cluster Autoscaler can set it accordingly? Ideally, we'd also like to get this backported as far as possible (the change was introduced in 1.24).

>  For this particular issue, UT (added in the PR) is able to catch it. And hence doesn't need to be that complicated to test with cluster-autoscaler.

Actually, the scheduler_perf has a test case `Unschedulable`. And, the scheduler_perf collects the `scheduler_scheduling_attempt_duration_seconds` metric ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1edbb8cf1a864c2dd71a1e5b7282de4bc3d8f5fa/test/integration/scheduler_perf/scheduler_perf_test.go#L87)), which has the `result` label in it ([ref](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/95bd687a284f63535cbf48b0696d8ae57c9929ef/pkg/scheduler/metrics/metrics.go#L65)). nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

Add one of the following kinds:
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

File system quota monitoring setup fails on subsequent invocations, each time quota setup is invoked a new random UID is generated for each pod and compared with the previously stored UID. 
This PR fixes it by keeping track of mapping between internal uid generated for a pod and actual external pod uid.
If there is already a quota project id associated with the folder it uses that instead of returning an error.
If quota is already set on a folder and the quota is the same it does an early exit.

title: Sandbox pause container not deleted
body:
### What happened?

A pod deletion did not result in the correct sandbox pause container being deleted. This was found during internal EKS testing on 1.22, where the test case was as follows:
1. Create a deployment with ~20 replicas and target a single Linux node.
2. Wait for all pods to have networking resources allocated
3. Delete the deployment
4. Validate that networking resources are cleaned up

What is unique about this test is that each pod sandbox fails to get an IP address assigned on average ~100 times before succeeding. So kubelet keeps trying to setup a pod sandbox using a new container ID each time. In the failure scenario, when kubelet finally sees the CNI succeed and the pod starts, it appears that kubelet is tracking an old container ID for the sandbox pod.

In the attached logs, the pod in question is `deployment-test-6655f9df8c-jc8gv`, and the sandbox create succeeds with container ID `49b6b37d511bcf993e0757afe45f55ee9d1ed2246834e055ba7f32fe7b20878e`, but kubelet appears to be tracking an old container ID, `c0fe93feba2615c06cac681f00b81d5e3a45ddab47714fbdb8bfc0d38253b720`.

When the pod is deleted, we never see a delete for the successful container ID, only the old container ID, and so the pod is cleaned up while the container remains running.

[eks_i-04f3b29e38d6f7a6e_2022-10-13_0346-UTC_0.7.1.tar.gz](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/9789136/eks_i-04f3b29e38d6f7a6e_2022-10-13_0346-UTC_0.7.1.tar.gz)


### What did you expect to happen?

I expect pod deletion to delete all sandbox pods. In this case, I expected a delete for `49b6b37d511bcf993e0757afe45f55ee9d1ed2246834e055ba7f32fe7b20878e` to be issued.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This is the challenging part. The steps we used to reproduce this with a 1/3 success rate were:
1. Create a deployment with ~20 replicas and set node affinity to a single Linux node
2. Configure CNI such that pods fail to get IP addresses for some time as CNI warms up
3. Delete deployment as soon as all pods are running successfully

### Anything else we need to know?

So far, we have only been able to reproduce this on 1.22. We were able to reproduce with kubelet logging verbosity set to 10, but enabling any containerd debug logging resulted in this not being reproducible. From the resulting logs, we were unable to confirm whether this was a kubelet or containerd issue.

Also, this issue does seem similar to [#110181. ](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/110181).

title: Discovery memCacheClient has inconsistent error behavior with other DiscoveryInterfaces
body:
### What happened?

I think this got stale and closed because it was posted on `kubernetes/client-go` but is still very relevant:
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/issues/745

The [memCacheClient](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/f81a9405fae9d2a97f479bab1ab540fad1d2f178/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L47) created by memory.NewMemCacheClient(...) returns an error when calling ServerResourcesForGroupVersion if the APIResources list returned is empty, as seen here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/6d14209323d355841b67c4d9ca8c22fb1ca930a6/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L214-L216

Our particular case came up due to the `external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1` API group being registered with the API server, but having no resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

If using [NewMemcachedDiscoveryClient](https://github.com/kubecfg/kubecfg/blob/4b23b794b8281c7886b5fd0bd03d7a38db876c10/cmd/root.go#L425) like [here](https://github.com/kubecfg/kubecfg/blob/4b23b794b8281c7886b5fd0bd03d7a38db876c10/pkg/kubecfg/validate.go#L48) to discover `apiservices` with zero current resources there should not be an error returned.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Do a discovery with a [memCacheClient](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/blob/f81a9405fae9d2a97f479bab1ab540fad1d2f178/discovery/cached/memory/memcache.go#L47) against a Kubernetes cluster that has at least one `apiservice` with zero resources. The condition on the server that triggers the described issue can be expressed as e.g.:
```
$ kubectl get --raw /apis/external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1
{"kind": "APIResourceList","apiVersion":"v1","groupVersion":"external.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1","resources":[]}
```

### Anything else we need to know?

I would be good to get to know the reasoning behind the emptiness check in the `memCacheClient`, maybe there is good reason for it.

<details>
Client Version: v1.20.15
Server Version: v1.22.8-gke.202

Reviving this issue based on https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/custom-metrics-apiserver/issues/146.

This behavior has become quite annoying for the custom/external metrics aggregated APIs since after https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/b8fe2c7b8061e6ab0b093a49351bac256606da4a, client-go is now producing a very spammy error log when an aggregated API is found without resource.

This is a very common scenario with the metric APIs since metrics are dynamically registered as Resources to the aggregated APIs so on startup the aggregated apiserver may not expose any resource and that's completely normal. It is even more common for implementations of these APIs that register metric Resources from CRDs as CRs tend to be created later than APIServices and the aggregated apiserver.

I can see a few path forward to improve the situation for us:
1. Remove the error if we consider that having no resources exposed by an aggregated API is acceptable
2. Increase the verbosity of the log to just show it in debugging scenarios
3. We somehow update https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/custom-metrics-apiserver/ to defer registration until we have at least one Metric resource.

@deads2k could you perhaps share your insight on that one please?

/remove-lifecycle stale

Hello folks!
Any update on this topic? The message is really spammy

Removing triage accepted manually since there was no update on this for more than 6 months.

/remove-triage accepted

For context, I traced it back and `len(r.APIResources) == 0` check has been considered an error since the first iteration of the in-memory discovery client in #48502:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8e7db3a0d34399e8235daed4b20abcd222cf1b34/pkg/controller/garbagecollector/memcachediscovery/client.go#L143-L150

It is unexpected for a built-in or CRD groupversion to have no resources, but for aggregated-apiservice I can see it being possible that the `APIService` object is created and set up for discovery before the aggregated-apiservice is ready.

I think this is [the commit in kube-client](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/commit/25d5761bfa0603c77cf5efefb14fd2e63a03a773) which introduces [the error we are facing in KEDA](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/custom-metrics-apiserver/issues/146) (but maybe I'm wrong).  
There is also [an issue](https://github.com/kubernetes/client-go/issues/1223) in that repo about the same issue after upgrading the kube-client pkg. [Could the option I suggested](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/custom-metrics-apiserver/issues/146#issuecomment-1402467093) in custom-metrics repo be correct from Kubernetes pov?
IMO we need to find a solution soon or the amount of noise will increase once people bump their deps and tooling ([helm is affected](https://github.com/helm/helm/issues/11772), kubectl is affected, and any tool which uses kube-client is affected)

title: containerd pod and mirror pods sometimes remain after deleting the manifest
body:
### What happened?

We have a test that creates a static pod on every node and a daemonset that later deletes the manifests for those files.  Sometimes the mirror pod and the containerd pod remain.  We've seen this when transient failures communicating with the apiserver caused a failure in calico like:
```
Oct 19 07:20:46 test-c5n6fr7206hepim5325g-kubee2epvgl-compute-000005fe kubelet.service[6774]: I1019 07:20:46.701627    6774 kubelet.go:2063] "SyncLoop REMOVE" source="file" pods=[pvg-k8s-psp-ns/static-nginx-10.184.98.11]

nodes.title: kubelet: Force deleted pods can fail to move out of terminating
nodes.body:
If a CRI error occurs during the terminating phase after a pod is force deleted (API or static) then the housekeeping loop will not deliver updates to the pod worker which prevents the pod's state machine from progressing.

Alter the housekeeping loop to always deliver updates to the pod worker when a pod is no longer in the config list, but only request aggressive termination when the pod is unknown to the pod worker, is not yet started, or has already terminated.

Why this fix?  HandlePodCleanups is responsible for performing a resync (in controller terminology): ensuring the pod worker, the kubelet config, and the container runtime state are in agreement.  The kubelet config loop (syncLoop and descendants) is responsible for triggering the pod worker state machine when new state is observed (either new config, new status, or retries the pod worker initiated by adding to the work queue).  The previous code stopped handling non terminal pods after a force deletion (pod no longer visible in config), which meant the pod worker no longer received the necessary triggers.  The pod worker detected the syncTerminatingPod error, queued the pod for retry on the work queue, and then waited forever for the config loop to tell the cleanup loop to converge.  In general, terminating errors are rare, and errors during sync are common, but as long as the pod remained in config periodic triggers from status would be sent.  We likely simply did not notice these zombies because force deletion is uncommon in prod environments and we don’t check for zombie pods in our test runs where force deletion is common. After this change, all missing pods trigger the pod worker every cleanup interval (every 2s), no matter their state.  The previous code was always wrong but we don’t have enough failure mode testing in e2e (cri is assumed to succeed, and we don’t query the kubelet to check for force deleted pod state).

/kind bug
/sig node
/priority important-soon

Fixes #105790, #109596, #113065, #113091, #113200, #113522, #115442

TODO:
* [x] unit tests - we have none for HandlePodCleanups
* [x] more involved test that reproduces the problem (e2e/integration/or unit)?
* [x] a metric?
* [x] add a unit test for verifying that static pods restart
* [x] add a unit test verifying that injecting a running pod update correctly drives a pod worker

```release-note
Force deleted pods may fail to terminate until the kubelet is restarted when the container runtime returns an error during termination. We have strengthened testing for runtime failures and now perform a more rigorous reconciliation to ensure static pods (especially those that use fixed UIDs) are restarted.  As a side effect of these changes static pods will be restarted with lower latency than before (2s vs 4s, on average) and rapid updates to pod configuration should take effect sooner.

A new metric `kubelet_known_pods` has been added at ALPHA stability to report the number of pods a Kubelet is tracking in a number of internal states.  Operators may use the metrics to track an excess of pods in the orphaned state that may not be completing.
```

title: Improve readiness times for clusters that use envelope encryption and create large numbers of secrets.
body:
**What would you like to be added**:
Remove the need to call remote KMS for every new Secret.

**Why is this needed**:
Due to the serial processing of List requests, the initialization of informers may take significant time due to the large number of consecutive trips to KMS. For example, assuming a 40 milliseconds round-trip to a KMS and two thousand secrets, the initialization of an informer may take 80 seconds.

Relevant PRs:
Reduce the number of trips to KMS by caching DEKs. #87438
Transform from storage concurrently during List operation. #88633

nodes.body: /sig auth
/assign @immutableT

Breaking the problem up a bit, we can reduce the number of calls across two boundaries:

1. kube-apiserver -> kms plugin
2. kms plugin -> non-local kms

Most ideas are around DEK reuse. Writing down notes from the brainstorm:

### Boundary 1

We've discussed a lot of options. I like the idea of keeping the DEKs one to one with objects, but reusing DEKs to encrypt the same object. If we use a counter to generate nonces (vs generating nonces randomly), we don't have to worry about the birthday problem and can switch to AES-GCM for data encryption without concern.

### Boundary 2

Plugins can reduce calls to remote KMS services by implementing a multi level KEK hierarchy. I.e. a plugin keeps local KEKs that it reuses across DEKs for some number of operations.

With ad hoc symbolic notation for operations:

```
| = concatenate
kid(key) -> key identifier
enc(key, data) -> cipher text
dec(key, cipher text) -> data
```

For an example key hierarchy:

![Key Hierarchy](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1787169/81361125-66a5fa80-9092-11ea-8df8-24e2f00ca9d9.png)

object_0_0_1 is stored as:

```
kid(kek_0) | enc(kek_0, kek_0_0) \
| kid(kek_0_0) | enc(kek_0_0, dek_0_0_1) \
| kid(dek_0_0_1) | enc(dek_0_0_1, object_0_0_1)
```
@enj @kubernetes/sig-auth-bugs

I am adding some background on GCM to help us navigate the decision on approach - caching DEK vs.  hierarchical key structure (as suggested by @mikedanese). 
 
From [NIST 800-38D](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38d.pdf) (emphasis and omissions are mine):
### Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC.
- The total number of invocations of the authenticated encryption function shall not exceed
**2^32** ... with the given key. 

**My interpretation of the above (in the context of envelope encryption feature):**
Given the upper limit of 2^32 invocations, it is safe cache DEKs when:

1. TTL is in the range of minutes (very conservative)
2. IV is produced via /dev/urandom (or via a counter as suggested by @mikedanese). 

Note that setting the cache TTL in the range of several minutes will dramatically reduce the number of trips to KMS since requests for Secrets creation are typically batched (ex. cluster creation or service deployment). The drawback of caching DEKs is that uses would need to wait for the duration of the cache TTL before performing storage migration.

I am adding PCI DSS requirements relevant to the protection of secrets at rest:

**3.5.3 Store secret and private keys used to encrypt/decrypt cardholder data in one (or more) of the following forms at all times**:

- Encrypted with a key-encrypting key that is at least as strong as the data encrypting key, and that is stored separately from the data-encrypting key

- Within a secure cryptographic device (such as a hardware (host) security module (HSM) or PTS approved point-of-interaction device)

- As at least two full-length key components or key shares, in accordance with an industry accepted method  

**3.6.4 Cryptographic key changes for keys that have reached the end of their crypto period** (for example, after a defined period of time has passed and/or after a certain amount of cipher-text has been produced by a given key), **as defined by the associated application vendor or key owner**, and based on industry best practices and guidelines (for example, NIST Special Publication 800-57). 

**3.6.5 Retirement or replacement (for example, archiving, destruction, and/or revocation) of keys as deemed necessary when the integrity of the key has been weakened** (for example, departure of an employee with knowledge of a clear-text key component), or keys are suspected of being compromised.

So I tried reading the hierarchical key structure but I will admit I am unable to parse what the image is trying to say ...

---

@immutableT would it be valuable to perform this experiment:

1. Create a cluster with KMS configured (to some cloud KMS) and create a large number of encrypted at rest secrets (100k?)
1. Set KMS `cachesize` cache size to > 100k
1. Restart cluster
1. Measure start up time
1. Calculate mean and standard deviation of gRPC calls.  This will give us the overhead of `kube-apiserver -> kms plugin` + `kms plugin -> non-local kms` calls.

Perform the same experiment but change the KMS to https://github.com/enj/citadel with a static KEK (i.e. `echo $secret_key`).  This will give us a good idea of what the overhead of the `kube-apiserver -> kms plugin` calls.

We can then determine `kube-apiserver -> kms plugin` vs. `kms plugin -> non-local kms` overhead.  In particular, it would tell us if a KMS plugin proxy that caches a KEK temporarily is viable or if we need to make changes directly to the API server.

Yes it would be. Furthermore, I think it would be a useful metric to have (see #91119).

While I am working on this experiment, I can provide some rough numbers based on my environment.
Since we measure the latency at both points: kube-apiserver and kms-plugin, by subtracting the median latency at kube-aipserver from that of kms-plugin, I estimated the overhead of over the Unix Domain Socket communications to be 6 ms for encrypt requests.

nodes.title: kmsv2: re-use DEK while key ID is unchanged
nodes.body:
This change updates KMS v2 to not create a new DEK for every
encryption.  Instead, we re-use the DEK while the key ID is stable.

Specifically:

We no longer use a random 12 byte nonce per encryption.  Instead, we
use both a random 4 byte nonce and an 8 byte nonce set via an atomic
counter.  Since each DEK is randomly generated and never re-used,
the combination of DEK and counter are always unique.  Thus there
can never be a nonce collision.  AES GCM strongly encourages the use
of a 12 byte nonce, hence the additional 4 byte random nonce.  We
could leave those 4 bytes set to all zeros, but there is no harm in
setting them to random data (it may help in some edge cases such as
live VM migration).

If the plugin is not healthy, the last DEK will be used for
encryption for up to three minutes (there is no difference on the
behavior of reads which have always used the DEK cache).  This will
reduce the impact of a short plugin outage while making it easy to
perform storage migration after a key ID change (i.e. simply wait
ten minutes after the key ID change before starting the migration).

The DEK rotation cycle is performed in sync with the KMS v2 status
poll thus we always have the correct information to determine if a
read is stale in regards to storage migration.

Signed-off-by: Monis Khan <mok@microsoft.com>

/kind feature
/kind api-change

Fixes: #90856

xref: #87438

```release-note
The API server now re-uses data encryption keys while the kms v2 plugin's key ID is stable.  Data encryption keys are still randomly generated on server start but an atomic counter is used to prevent nonce collisions.
```

title: If kubelet is unavailable, AttachDetachController fails to force detach on pod deletion
body:
/kind bug

**What you expected to happen**:
When a pod using an attached volume is deleted (gracefully) but kubelet in the corresponding node is down, the AttachDetachController should assume the node is unrecoverable after a timeout (currently 6min) and forcefully detach the volume. 

**What happened**:
The volume is never detached.

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:
* Create a pod with a volume using any of the attachable plugins (I used GCE PD to test).
* Stop kubelet inside the node where the pod is scheduled.
* Delete the pod.
* Wait for 6min+
* Check to see if the volume is still attached.

**Anything else we need to know?**:
This doesn't happen if the pod is force-deleted.

It's likely due to the last condition checked in [this line](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5e9a5659b751bd1d765758548273198fe8e40642/pkg/volume/util/util.go#L649). Once kubelet is down, the container  status is no longer reported correctly. Inside the Attach Detach Controller, This function is called by the pod update informer handler, which sets whether the volume should be attached in the desired state of the world. On pod force deletion, the pod object is deleted immediately, and this triggers the pod delete informer handler, which doesn't call this function.

/sig storage
/cc @saad-ali @gnufied @jingxu97 @NickrenREN 
/assign

@saad-ali, @verult  and I scheduled a meeting to talk about this issue on Monday 27Aug 11am (New York, USA Time).

Hi @saad-ali , @verult and @gnufied.

I have a concern about how to fix this issue.
Regarding the implementation of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67847 \ https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67419 , I am not sure if the PR design is save enough.
The solution that was proposed in this PR was to leverage the DeletionGracePeriodSeconds instead of using the podStatus.ContainerStatuses ([HERE](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5e9a5659b751bd1d765758548273198fe8e40642/pkg/volume/util/util.go#L649)).

Its good not to trust on podStatus.ContainerStatuses because in a crash worker scenario the kubelet is not responsive and the ContainerStatuses will remain Running for-ever (which prevent detach the POD). So adding DeletionGracePeriodSeconds as another trigger to force detach the PVCs of a none responding POD is good idea.

BUT I think we should be very careful of force detach PVCs,  because if its a split brain scenario (worker node was not really crashed, it was just a network issue) and the POD still running and writing IO to the PVC, detaching the PVC may lead to data corruption.
So maybe its too brutal to trust on this DeletionGracePeriodSeconds (AFAIK the customer facing of this timeout is TerminationGracePeriodSeconds which is by default 30 seconds if you didn't specify it in the pod spec.).   So if we take this PR implementation there could be application that will get force detach in split brain and maybe these application cannot handle such detach.

I would like to propose saver implementation that from one hand will do detach for PODs that in crashed node scenario, but from other hand will be save enough also for split brain scenario.
The propose is to add a new annotation on the POD spec (e.g : AllowForceDetachAfterGracePeriod with default false), and then only if the customer specify it in the pod spec with true value,
 then k8s will force detach PVCs of this POD, but if its false then even after DeletionGracePeriodSeconds it will not force detach the POD - which keeping the existing behavior - so customer will have to manually delete the POD (do it in save and manual way to prevent data lose).
So by adding this safety annotation we provide the customer the ability to decide if this pod can recover from detach operation. And then you will fill save to also chary pick this fix to older k8s versions, because you will not impact any existing behavior(Only PODs with this annotation will get the new behavior).

Thoughts?   
Let me know if its over kill, or maybe its saver for the user to avoid potential data lose.

One of the other things we could do is - only detach volumes from a node when it is known that it has been shutdown. So basically make use of newly introduced taint to detach the volume. This does mean that volumes never get detached from unresponsive or crashed kubelet nodes but that is probably fine. If user really wants to force the detach he can always do that via:

```
~> kubectl delete pod <foo> --force=true --grace-period=0
```
This will mean, we will have to roll this PR into https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67977 and we obviously can't backport. 

Older versions of AWS, Openstack and Vsphere is not affected by this bug btw - because in those cloudproviders a node is deleted when shutdown. It is only recently that this behaviour was changed in those cloud providers and node object no longer is deleted and hence pods remain in "Unknown" phase and volume *never* gets detached. 

This bug affects  versions as far back as 1.9 (or even before that). But cloudprovider behaviour is recent change. Another problem is - using shutdown to detect volume detach has been feature gated as an alpha feature, 

I do not like annotation option that much tbh. It is hard to document and easy to miss and since it is an API change, it also has to go through alpha, beta phases. Agreed that - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67977 is currently feature gated too but I do not see a strong reason of why that should be feature gated. cc @yastij
@gnufied - some production cluster relies on quick reboots (i.e. reboot and still have disks attached). We might want to give them some bandwidth for transition.

@yastij shouldn't pod eviction timeout(5 minute default) + expiry window before a node is considered lost and it stops sending heartbeats enough? There is also - grace period obviously.

The reason I do not particularly like annotation also is because, detaching volumes from shutdown nodes should be a default behavior and should not require user intervention. If we can differentiate between shutdown nodes and unresponsive kubelets then we should use that information for detaching volumes and it should be default rather than something that user have to configure.

I agree with @gnufied on annotations.

the plan is to promote this as beta on 1.13. From what I’ve see the eviction timeout impacts **all pods** which might be tricky: for aggresive clusters this doesn’t work as pod timeout and node grace period are set lower than usual. This window (1 release) ensures that everything goes smoothly.

Good arguments on both sides. On the one hand, we have to very careful not to cause data corruption. On the other hand, we don't want to get in to a state where their data is stuck and requires manual intervention to access from new workloads.

I agree with @gnufied, we should avoid adding another annotation -- whenever there is a question like this, exposing the option to the end user is the easiest way out, but not necessarily the best. We should try to be smart and do the right thing automatically on behalf of the user.

The right thing in this case is tricky. If a node is not coming back, we should move the disk even if it is not safely unmounted. But how do we differentiate that from a split brain? A timer based algorithm is pretty crude, but its the best approximation we currently have. And I'm not aware of any way to detect a split brain vs a dead node so I think we need to weigh the likely hood of the different scenarios happening and the worst case for each option and how willing we are to tolerate that.

I'll leave it up to you guys to weigh those tradeoffs.

@gnufied actually in openstack nodes are not deleted anymore. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/59931 It basically means that in openstack if you shutdown instance which had pod with pvc, it cannot failover to another instance.

However, #67977 will fix this issue

I just talked to @yastij that we should use feature gate only to detach delay. Then it can detach volumes in openstack again, if feature gate turned on the delay is something like 1min and if not turned on the detach delay is something like 8-10minutes. 

You are correct like in AWS this problem does not exist but if #59930 is approved (like it should because other cloud behaviour and spec is that it should not delete nodes). Then aws will get this problem as well if #67977 is not approved.

Some notes I took during the conference meeting today (@verult  please add your notes as well):

- PRs https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67847, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67419 should be on hold, due to the potential risk in split brain situation. And as for now the user will have to manually delete the Pods from the crashed node or just delete the crash node object in order to trigger PVC detach operation.

- PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67977 is still in place, because it will allow detach PVCs from node with nodeShutdown taint.  But its only applicable for cloud provider drivers. 

- Opened ticket https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/68086 to make maxWaitForUnmountDuration as configurable value (instead of hardcoded 6 minutes).

- Its less recommended to use Pod annotation to indicate force detach PVC mode.

Do we have any notion of the timeframe on resolving this issue? Code freeze is next week, at which point only critical/urgent bugs will be permitted into the milestone.

Thank you! :)

@shay-berman PR #67977 should still be on hold because without actual handling of pods from shutdown nodes the PR #67977 has no effect whatsoever. The volumes still will not be detached from shutdown nodes.

cc @msau42 @jingxu97

@zetaab dangling error should just add a volume to actual state of the world to handle the case of missed pod statuses. In itself - it should *never* cause volume detaches. If it does, we probably have a bug. I have tested similar scenario on AWS with latest patch(https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/66835)  that prevents node object from being deleted and volumes are NOT detached. 

If on openstack volumes are being detached from a shutdown nodes with pod objects still being around, then I would call it magic/bug. :-)

Lets think following scenario: I have pod with pvc located in node1, that node crashes and it cannot start anymore. How the kubernetes should behave?

- do nothing: wait until admin comes online (admin can for instance detach volume manually, and then pod will start in another node. Or he can just delete the broken machine, and volume is detached. Automation can also delete machines?)

Just to add to what @shay-berman wrote the complete discussion is as follows:

1. Both https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67977 and https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67847 should be on hold for now. Because as we discovered that #67977 will have no effect if pod is not being removed from DSWP(desired state of the world).

2. The reason we chose to put https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/67847 on hold is because, any timing value we decide for force detaching volume from a pod in "Unknown" phase is fundamentally unsafe.  This was recommendation from @derekwaynecarr and @liggitt too.

3. We also discussed possibility of using "Shutdown" taint for removing pods from DSWP. The underlying idea is - if a node has "Shutdown" taint then all its pods that are either fully terminated or have DeletionTimeStamp set could be removed from DSWP and hence trigger detach.  The problem with doing this in attach/detach controller is - attach/detach controller should use pod's status as single source of truth for performing detaches. It was pointed to us that stateful sets and replication controller backed pods may need to be special cased and hence if volumes MUST be detached from a node that is shutdown, that decision should be based on pod's status and should come from node/pod lifecycle controller.  For example - in future node lifecycler controller may mark containers of a pod that are on a shutdown/poweredoff node as terminated/not running and hence attach/detach controller will automatically detach volumes from it.  @derekwaynecarr @liggitt had some valid points against special casing this in attach/detach controller.
@shay-berman the PR we were going to keep was this one that already merged, which introduces the node shutdown taint: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/59323

@jingxu97 @msau42 and @random-liu from sig-node discussed offline about potentially having a higher level controller to force delete a pod. One of the possible issues is that there could be a race condition if the node comes back up soon after.

Imagine we have a StatefulSet pod that has a non-attachable volume, and suppose the shutdown node comes back up right before the pod is force deleted. Kubelet on the node sees the pod is still scheduled on it and starts the containers. Then the pod is force deleted, and a new pod gets started on a different node. Now there's a chance the same containers are running on both nodes.

For intentional shutdown of a node for maintenance, where highly responsive transfer of workloads to another node is desired, there's no substitute for cordoning/draining workloads from the node prior to shutdown.

Is the desire here to handle intentionally shutting down a node without terminating it, and without cordoning/draining it, while still quickly moving workloads and volumes to another node?
@liggitt - Yes, it may also cover shutting down a node when it may need to be migrated and re-deployed.
For an intentional shutdown of a node, how come a node drain cannot be done?
